lectures.title: DynamoDB Security & Other
lectures.text:
So one let's talk about, DynamoDB security and some other features. So for security, we have VPC endpoints that are going to be available to access DynamoDB without using the public internet, and only keeping all the traffic within your VPC. Access to DynamoDB is fully controlled by IAM, which makes it a great database choice in AWS. And you have encryption at rest using AWS KMS or in-transit using SSL and TLS. There are backup and restore features available.

You have two of them. So you have point-in-time recovery, so PITR, just like RDS and there's no performance impacts, or we can just do a normal backup and restore it. Now there's the concept of global tables and DynamoDB. So the idea is that you have a multi-region, multi-active fully replicated high-performance table in DynamoDB. And how to enable it? Well, you need to first enable DynamoDB streams. So, while DynamoDB is a cloud service, It's possible for you to get a simulation of DynamoDB on your local computer, called DynamoDB local, and the idea is that you have, a local DynamoDB database that you can use to develop and test your applications locally without using the DynamoDB web service, which is really, really handy.

And if you wanted to migrate data to and from DynamoDB, the AWS Database Migration Service is a great choice. So for example, from MongoDB to DynamoDB, or Dynamic V2 Oracle, mySQL, S3 and so on. Now another feature you need to understand around DynamoDB is going to be around fine grain access. So for example, if you have clients and applications, web, or mobile, and they need to access directly our DynamoDB table, then we don't want to give them IAM permissions and IAM roles, users directly from AWS, that will be truly inefficient and a security hole.

Instead, we're going to use an identity provider. It could be Amazon Cognito User Pools, Google login, Facebook login, open ID connect, or SAML or whatever. And the users will, in the simplified flow, login with these identity providers and they will have the feature to exchange the credentials they just got for temporary AWS credentials. And the idea is that because they're temporary, they're more secure. And with them, they can be associated with an IAM role, but this IAM role must be restricted because now that our clients and applications can access our DynamoDB table, you want them to be able to do operations only on the data that they own.

And so how do we do this, this fine grain access control? Well, we have a federated login to get temporary credentials, and then we can create IAM role, and this IAM role will have a condition. And this condition will lead on to what the user can do. So here is a sample policy. So in this policy, the user can do get item, batch get item, query, put item, update item, delete item and batch right item on a specific table. But there's a condition here.

And the condition is saying, Hey, only if the leading keys is corresponding to DynamoDB and then the connector identity pseudo variables, which will be replaced at run time by the specific user. And so effectively what we're saying is that with LeadingKey, we only limit row level access for users based on what the primary key value is. And so therefore we make sure that the users can only modify and access their own data. And you can also specify conditions on attributes and this would be to limit the specific attributes a user can see in your DynamoDB table, okay?

So to summarize, you have fine-grain access control by using a federated login and by specifying a condition on LeadingKeys, if you want it to limit at the role level or attributes, if you want your limits at the column level, the attribute level. Okay, that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it. And I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: API Gateway Overview
lectures.text:
So, so far in our serverless journey, we've seen how to create Lambda functions and we've seen how to use DynamoDB. And so the functions can use DynamoDB as a database for our API, and we can do create, read, update, delete on our tables, but we'd like our clients to be able to invoke this Lambda function in some way. So there are multiple of doing it. We can have the client directly invoke the Lambda function, but that means that the client would need IAM permissions, or we've seen we can use an application load balancer to have it in between the client and the Lambda function and that would expose our Lambda function as an HTTP endpoint.

There's one last thing we can use. It's called the API Gateway. And this is a serverless offering from AWS which allows us to create REST APIs that are going to be public and accessible for our clients. So the client will talk to the API Gateway and the beautiful things that the API Gateway will then proxy the request to our Lambda functions. So it would use an API Gateway because it provides us more than just an HTTP endpoint. It will provide us a lot of features as we'll see in this section, such as authentication, such as usage plans, development stages and all that kind of things.

So the API Gateway has a lot of features and this is just an overview, but we can integrate the API Gateway and Lambda and that gives us a full serverless application. So no infrastructure to manage. We have support for the WebSocket Protocol so we can do real-time streaming through the API Gateway in two different ways. The API Gateway handle API versioning. So we can go from version one to version two and version three and not break our clients.

We can handle multiple environments that includes a dev, a test and the prod environment. There is a whole thing about API Gateway and security. So there's a tons of way to enable security on your API Gateway for both authentication and authorization. We have the ability to create API keys, do request throttling in case some clients are doing too many requests on our API Gateway, and we can also use some common standards such as Swagger or Open API 3.0 to import quickly defined APIs, and also we can export them as Swagger and Open API.

We can transform and validate request and response in the API Gateway level to ensure that the invocation are correct, and we can generate SDK and API specifications and cache API responses. So lots of features that come with the API Gateway that are not necessarily included when you use something as simple as an application load balancer. So what is the API Gateway integrate with? Well, there is a Lambda function and we've seen this from the previous diagram, so it can invoke a Lambda function.

And with this integration, it is the most common way and a very easy way to expose REST a API backed by a Lambda function to do a full serverless application. But also HTTP. So we can expose any HTTP endpoints in the backend. So it could be, for example, an HTTP API you have on premises, or it could be an application load balancer you have on your cloud environment. And why would you do this? Well, you would use an API Gateway to leverage the rate limiting features, the caching, the user authentication, the API keys, et cetera.

So it's definitely used full to have a layer of API Gateway on top of your HTTP endpoint. And finally, we can use an evidence service so we can expose any AWS API through the API Gateway. So which ones, for example, where we can start a Step Function workflow, we can post a message to SQS directly from an API Gateway API. Why would you do this? Well, because maybe you want to add authentication, deploy some APIs publicly or do some rate control on some AWS services.

So here is an example of the API Gateway used with an AWS service. So example, Kinesis Data Streams. So we want to have people send data into a Kinesis Data Streams but in a secure way, without giving them access to AWS credentials. So what we do is that's in between our clients and our Kinesis Data Streams, we're going to have the API Gateway. And the clients will send HTTP request into the API Gateway. And it's been configured to then send the messages into a Kinesis Data Streams.

And as you see in this setting, we don't manage any servers. Then Kinesis Data Stream from there, we can, for example, send the records into a Kinesis Data Firehose and eventually put them into an Amazon S3 bucket in the JSON format. So you start to see the power of API Gateway. You can actually expose any AWS service to the outside through an API Gateway. There are three ways to deploy your API Gateway. This is called endpoint types. So the first type, which is the default one is called Edge-Optimized.

This is for your global clients. So that means that your API Gateway is going to be accessible from anywhere in the world. And to be efficient, the request are going to be routed through all the CloudFront Edge locations, which will improve the latency. Your API Gateway is still only in one region where you created it, but it's accessible efficiently from every CloudFormation Edge location. Then there's a regional deployment. So this is when we don't want to use CloudFront Edge locations.

So it's when we expect all our users to be within the same region where we created our API Gateway. And if you wanted to, you could create your own platform distribution, and this will give you the same result as an Edge-Optimized distribution, but this time you have more control over location strategies and the platform settings themselves. And then finally, the last kind of API Gateway you can do is a private API Gateway. So this time it's not public.

lectures.title: API Gateway Stages and Deployment
lectures.text:
So we have deployed our first API through the API Gateway in a deployment stage. So what we've seen is that whenever we made changes to the API Gateway, they were not effective until we did a deployment. So we need to make a deployment for them to be in effect. And it's a common source of confusion. Some people will go and change how the API works, but forget to do a deployment and therefore the API will not be live. So these changes are deployed to stages and you can have as many stages as you want and you can use the naming you want.

For example, you can use a dev, test, and prod stage or a v1, v2, v3 whatever you want to do. And each stage will get its own configuration parameters and they can be rolled back seamlessly because a whole history of all the deployments that have happened onto a stage is kept. So let's take the example of we have two stages and we're creating a breaking API change. So our Lambda function backing our API Gateway is going to change. So we have the v1 stage and it invokes the v1 function and we've deployed it and so our v1 clients are going to be able to access our API through this URL.

But we are programming a new version of our Lambda function called v2. And this v2 does not respect the same format of data and so on and so we know that if we deploy the changes on the v1 stage, it will break our v1 clients. So what we do is then instead we decide to create a new stage, call it the v2 stage, pointing to the v2 function. And this will create a new URL. So now the api.example.com/v2, which represents the v2 stage. And the cool thing is that our clients can now be updated to version two and access this new URL, and we can maintain compatibility.

So for a while, the v1 and the v2 can coexist together as two different stages. We can migrate the clients from the version one to the version two and then when no more clients are using the version one, then we can shut it down and move on with our API Gateway. So this is a very common use cases for stages. Now, how do we expand this? We can use stage variables. So stage variables are just like environment variables, but for the API Gateway stages.

And you use them to change configuration values without redeploying your API. Okay, so now I want to show you stage variables. So to do this, we're going to create a resource, named "stage variables." And we're going to test out stage variables in there. So before we create a method, we need to author a Lambda function, and we're going to author several versions for our Lambda function. So this one is going to be api-gateway-stage-variables-get, and the runtime is going to be, again, Python 3.11. What we're going to do is that we're going to create code for it, and author versions, version one, version two, et cetera.

We're going to create aliases, to map these versions to aliases, and then we're going to invoke these aliases directly from the API gateway. So let's copy this code again, and paste it in. And the first one is going to be "Hello from Lambda v1." So we're going to test it with the test events right now just make sure we get the outcome we want. So we need to deploy it to get the right changes. Let's test it again. So we get "Hello from Lambda v1."

This is perfect. So now we're going to actually create a new version out of it. So to do so, action, and then publish new version. This is v1, and let's publish it. So now we have version one created, and it says "Hello from Lambda v1." So now we're going to update this code again. So for this, I need to switch versions. So let's go back into our function right here. And we're going to do "Hello from Lambda v2." Again, we're going to deploy this, and we're going to test it.

So we get "Hello from Lambda v2." This is great. And again, we're gonna do action, and then publish new version. So this version is version two. Perfect. And finally, we are going to have a last one, which is going to be, so let's go back up one more time. We're going to go to our Lambda function code, and do "Hello from Lambda in DEV." And we're going to again, test this, deploy it, excuse me, then test it. It says "Hello from Lambda DEV," so that's perfect.

And then we're going to just not publish this version. This is going to be our latest one. So to summarize, we have three versions. So we have three versions of our function: We have v1, v2, and then latest. So now we need to create new aliases from it. So let's create an alias, and this one is going to be DEV. And DEV is always pointing to my latest version. So I'm going to say "point to latest." Then we're going to create another alias. So let's go back in here, and we're going to create another alias.

This one is going to be TEST, and the version is version two, because this is the newest version that we're testing right now. So we save this. So now if we invoke PROD, for example, if we were to test this PROD version, it would say "Hello from Lambda v1." And if we tested TEST, it'd be "Hello from v2," and DEV, "from DEV."

So now that we have our function with multiple aliases, it's time to map it to the API gateway. So it's complete the function ARN, go under API gateway, and then we're going to create a method of type get, for our Lambda function. And the Lambda function, we're going to choose proxy mode again, and we're going to paste this ARN, but then you add something, :${stageVariables.LambdaAlias}. And so here when we do this, the UI says, "Hey, you define your Lambda function as a stage variable."

And so you need to make sure the the function has enough permissions to run it. And so we have the permission command right here. So we are going to copy this, and we're going to open Cloud Shell to run this command. So let's wait for Cloud Shell to start. So now that my Cloud Shell is launched, I need to copy this statement, which has a bug in its current state. So I'm going to just show you what's wrong. But maybe by the time you do this, hands-on, it's not here, but the ARN is repeated twice.

So you just make sure if you have this bug, to remove this, so that it just has only one ARN and it starts by ARN. So on top of it, you remove this last part, from the dollar sign, and you add "DEV." And we're going to do it three times. So here we will allow our API gateway to invoke the DEV alias of our Lambda function. So let's paste that in, press enter, and it's done. Then we do it again. We change this for test, and we allow our API gateway to invoke the TEST alias of our Lambda function.

Perfect. And then lastly, for PROD, and we will allow our API gateway to invoke the PROD alias for our Lambda function. So this is done, and now I can go ahead and create my method. So we're good to go. And what we realize here, is that now if I go into my API gateway, look at my alias for example, let's look at the PROD alias. And we look at permissions, under configuration, we scroll down and we see that one resource-based policy statement was added, saying that the API gateway can invoke this PROD alias.

So this is the security part. So now let's go ahead, and verify that the PROD alias is working. So I'm going to click on Test. And under Test, for stage variables, of course, under Tests, you will find that there is a Lambda alias. And here you just enter PROD. And what this is going to do is that it's going to force this test to invoke the prod alias of our Lambda function. So let's test it. And we get a response 200, "Hello from Lambda v1." So this did invoke indeed, the PROD alias.

Now if we turn to test, it's going to test the TEST Lambda alias, and we get a "Hello from Lambda v2." And if we do DEV, then we test it, and we get a "Hello from Lambda DEV." So this is showing that this stage variable is now impacting which Lambda alias we are invoking. And this is the whole power of stage variables. So now let's deploy our API to DEV, and to other stages afterwards, to show you where to use the stage variables. So we have deployed our API into DEV, and I scroll down.

And in there, you can set up the stage variables. So you edit it, you add a new one, called lambdaAlias, and you set the value to DEV. So that means that for the stage DEV, this variable is going to be equal always to DEV. And so therefore, the Lambda function that's going to be invoked as my DEV alias. I can also create two other stages. So let's deploy this API twice. So we create a new stage called TEST. And in the TEST stage, I'm going to also manage variables, and have a lambdaAlias to be of TEST.

And finally, I'm going to deploy into PROD. So I'm going to create a new stage, call it "prod," deploy. And again, we are going to set this stage variable in prod, called lambdaAlias, of value "PROD," with capital letters. Okay. So once we have done that, we can test our deployment of the API. So I have copied my URL, I paste it, and I add "/stage-variables." And you see I get a "Hello from Lambda v1," because I'm in PROD. But if I change the URL, and have DEV, then I get "Hello from Lambda DEV," and if I change the URL, and add TEST, then I get "Hello from Lambda v2."

So as you can see, each stage is now linked to a specific LambdaAlias, through the usage of stage variables. And this is the whole power of it. So I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

So let's have a look at all the configuration options for your stage. So if you click on Stage details Edit, you can change the stage description. You can decide to have a cache, so it could be an API cache to cache the requests and the responses, and so therefore you need to configure it over time. And if you want to have firewall configuration and client certificate to verify that the requests are from API Gateway.

Next, we have logging and tracing. So you can set up logging tracing with CloudWatch Logs, for example, finding errors only or info logs or full request and response logs in case you need to debug everything, but this may display sensitive data. Detailed metrics or not, custom access logging if you wanted to, and extra tracing to have full integration between the API Gateway and X-Ray service. We also have stage variables as we saw before. Deployment history to see how many times you've deployed to your stage.

Documentation history in case you do manage documentation for your API. Canary, we'll see canary in a few lectures. And then tags where we can tag this stage itself. So that's it for all the configuration options for your stage. There are some that we'll see in detail in the future lectures so that we'll keep this one short. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: API Gateway Canary Deployments
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about a way to perform canary deployments on your API gateway. So the idea is that you want to enable a way to test a small amount of traffic on the change you have done on your API gateway. So usually it's done in production. So you would choose the amount of percent of traffic that the canary channel will receive and this would allow you to test your new version, for example of your API gateway, over the backend Lambda function or something like this.

So say our prod stage currently points to version one and our client wants to be able to test a new version. So we're going to create a prod stage canary for version two and what this will do is that we will be allowing our client to have for example 95% of the traffic that goes to the existing prod stage which we know works and behind the scenes automatically 5% of the traffic will go to the canary stage. From this, we can test all the changes, look at metrics, look at logs, look at everything, maybe debug see if everything is working, and when we're confident, we can just move over 100% of the traffic into your canary stage.

So in this example, the metrics and the logs will be separate, so this is for better monitoring. And you can override any stage variables you wanted for your canary stage and this is equivalent of performing blue/green deployment with Lambda and API gateway. So let's go into hands-on to see how that works.

lectures.title: API Gateway Canary Deployments Hands On
lectures.text:
So, let's demo the Canary. For this, I'm going to create a new resource and I will call it canary-demo and create this resource. Under it, I'm going to create a method of type GET of Lambda function with the proxy integration type, and I'm going to choose the Lambda function, which is the stage-variables-get function. Because we have a third in this function, we have a third, two versions, version one and version two. Version one is saying hello from v1 and version two is saying hello from v2.

So, we're now going to use stage variables in this one, we're just going to use the version one and version two of this function. So to point this to version one, you need to add a colon and then one to say that yes, we're going to invoke version one of this Lambda function. So, let's create this method. And as you can see now, canary-demo, if I try to test it and just test a method, I get back "Hello from Lambda v1." So, this is perfect. And now, I'm going to deploy this API into a stage.

It's going to be a new stage and I'll call this one canary, just to do the canary demo. Okay, so we are in canary now and if I try to access this invoke URL, /canary/ again canary, for a canary demo for the route that we just set up, we get a "Hello from Lambda v1." So, so far so good. But now what we're going to do is that we're going to set up a canary. So to do so, what I have to do is that I need to go into Canary here and I need to create a canary.

And we're seeing, hey, that the distribution request for the canary is going to be 50% for the canary and 50% for the current stage. So effectively, when you have a canary, you'll choose a much smaller percentage, for example, 10%. But because I want to show you how it works, I'm going to do 50/50. So once we have created a canary, then we are ready to deploy a new update to our stage. So for this, I go back to my resources, I go to my method, canary-demo, GET, and I will change the integration request.

I will edit it, and this time, instead of having version one, I will invoke version two. So I'm going to save this. And now, if we just do a quick test in here, as we can see, we get a "Hello from Lambda v2." So now let's deploy this API and I will choose Canary and deploy it. So now this has been deployed to Canary, and if I go to the Canary stage and go to Canary, now even though it's not showing that we've deployed something into Canary, it was before in the previous UI, now it doesn't.

Maybe it will after a UI update again. But if I go to my URL in here, my canary-demo, and refresh this page, as you can see, it does "Hello from Lambda v1" and then it switches to "Hello from Lambda v2." So that means that my Canary is switching between v1 and v2. So this is how we can test if your new API is working as expected. And then when you're done, you can just promote the canary to say, "Hey, you should update the stage with the canary deployment" and so on.

So let's do this. And now if I refresh this, I only see "Hello from Lambda" and it should just take a little bit of time. But now it's working and you only get "Hello from Lambda v2." lectures.title: API Gateway Integration Types & Mappings
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about the different ways we can integrate our API Gateway with our backend. And the first type is Integration Type MOCK which is just to return a response without even sending a request to the backend. So this is useful when you are programming your API Gateway and configuring it and you don't want to have any work on the backend just yet. So as you can expect, this is not something for production. This is something for just development and testing.

Then we have the HTTP, or AWS Lambda and other services in which the API Gateway will forward our request, but we can modify it. So we must both configure what's called an integration request and an integration response. And when you set that up, we can set up data mappings using mapping templates for the request and the response. Well, that means that we will be able to change the request made to the backend and to change the response back from the backend before sending it to our clients.

So this is really helpful. For example, if we create a REST API and our API Gateway and we add mapping templates and then we're going to map this REST API call to an API call on the SQS Queue by changing, renaming, reordering, all these kind of things such as the SQS Queue can understand the API call made by the API Gateway. So here, the API Gateway has the power to change the request and the response. Okay, this is not the things we've seen. We've seen so far the one integration called AWS Proxy, which means Lambda Proxy, in which the request from the client is going to be the input to the Lambda.

And we haven't modified any request or response because we cannot, it's a proxy. And so the function is solely responsible for the logic of the request and the response. That means that we cannot use any mapping templates, we cannot change the headers, the query string parameters. All these things will be passed as arguments to our function directly. And this is what we've seen. So when we logged in the Lambda, our request coming from the API Gateway, so we logged the event, we could see adjacent document that looked just like this.

So we have the information about the resource, the path, the HTTP method, the headers, the query string parameters and so on, as well as stage variables, the body and all these other things. So this is very helpful. And then our Lambda function is responsible to take this request, understand what to do with it and then the Lambda function can return a response. And we've framed a response like this as well. So we specify the status code, we specify the headers, as well as the body.

So here in this Proxy Integration, all the work is on the backend and the API Gateway is just here to proxy requests through. So there's a last integration type called HTTP Proxy. In which case, again because this is a proxy, we don't have any mapping templates and the request itself is passed directly, so proxy to the backend. And then when the backend replies, then the response is again proxied by the API to going back into the clients. And if you wanted to, you can add HTTP headers if you need be.

So for example, you can add an API key between your API Gateway and your backhand, but your users don't see it. So let's take an example, a client makes an HTTP request into your API Gateway. You're going to proxy that request to your backend, for example an Application Load Balancer. But again, as I said, you can add optional HTTP headers, such as an API key, that really guarantees that your API call is going to work. So the client does not need to know about the secret API key, but yet your backend will see it coming from the API Gateway.

So mapping templates to modify the request and the response, they are only applicable if we integrate within AWS or HTTP, but without using the proxy methods. So they can be used to modify request and response. And then with it, we are able to rename or modify query string parameters, to modify the body content, to add or modify headers. And to do this, it uses something called the VTL. So the Velocity Template Language which allows us to get for loops, if's, etc.

It's a scripting language used to modify some requests. And finally, when we receive response it is possible for us to remove some results out of the response by again using the mapping templates. Finally, to set the mapping templates, you must set the Content-Type to be application/json or application/xml. So a concrete application of a mapping template that can come up in the exam is how to integrate a client with a SOAP API through an API Gateway.

So what is a SOAP API? SOAP APIs are XML based and we know REST APIs they are JSON based. And so we need to have something in between to convert the JSON into XML and back. And so the idea is that you would create your API Gateway with a mapping template and the client would interact with JSON in your API Gateway. But your API Gateway, thanks to the mapping template, can transform this payload into an XML payload, into the SOAP API and back. And so in this case, the API Gateway should extract the data from the request, either the path, the payload, or the header, then build the SOAP message necessary for the backend to understand, so this is where we use the mapping template, then call the SOAP service and receive the XML response and finally transform the XML response back into a desired format to respond to your users.

Here is another example where we use the mapping template to use query string parameters. So our client is integrated with API Gateway which is using Lambda directly, not as a proxy. And so we want to be able to map the query string parameters, so if we send a request like this with a question mark, name equals foo and other equal bar, we want to be able to rename these query string parameters before passing into the Lambda so we can create a mapping template and then the JSON that gets passed into the Lambda function could be my variable foo and other variable bar.

And so in this example what I've done is that I've renamed variables so you can map them to anything you want. And this is again yet another use cases for your mapping templates. So that's it for the theory. Now let's go into the practice to see how they work.

lectures.title: API Gateway Open API
lectures.text:
So the API Gateway has a tight integration with the OpenAPI specification. So what is the OpenAPI specification? Well, it's a very common way to define REST APIs and the API definition itself is code. So what you can do is that you create this specification using the OpenAPI model 3.0 and then you import that into the API gateway. So you define the methods, the method request, the integration request, the method response, as well as any AWS extension that you can set up for the API gateway.

And you can set up every single option of these extensions directly from within the API spec. Similarly, instead of importing stuff into the API Gateway, you can take an existing API in the API Gateway and export it as an OpenAPI spec. Why? Well, because this specification can be used to, for example, generate client code. So these OpenAPI specifications can either be written in YAML or JSON, and then when you use them you can generate client SDKs as I've just mentioned.

So on top of having a one-to-one mapping between the API Gateway and the OpenAPI spec you can use the OpenAPI spec to perform request validation within your API gateway. So the idea is that, instead of just sending a payload as is to your backend, API Gateway can verify if it corresponds to a proper schema. And so in case it doesn't correspond to the correct validation, the caller gets directly a 400 error and that reduces unnecessary call to the backend.

So you can check whether or not the request parameters are in the URI, the query strings, you can test for headers that are present or not, and that they're non-blank. And then you can also have a look whether or not the payload adheres to a specified JSON Schema model for the method. So all now you can just verify that your backend will not have any issues with parsing and using that payload. So how do we do this? Well, we set up an OpenAPI definitions file, and in it we have an x-amazon-apigateway-request-validator.

And here we can define what we want to validate, the body, the parameters on all methods, on some methods, and so on. So you can enable params-only validator on all API methods, or you can, for example, enable all validators on just a POST /validation method, or whatever method you want. So you're really free to verify whatever you want on your API. So hopefully that makes sense. Hopefully you see the power of using OpenAPI with the API Gateway.

I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.text:
So let's go and see how we can first import an OpenAPI definition. So I'm going to create a new API. It's going to be a REST API, and I can click on imports. As you can see we have a new API called Pet Store, that has been created which contains the proper resources that we need to. And in stage action you can export it, so if you export it, you specify the format you want, is it swagger or OpenAPI 3, is it JSON or YAML?

And then do you want to have the extensions of OpenAPI gateway and Postman? So lots of options. lectures.title: API Gateway Caching
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about how we can enable caching of our responses in the API gateway. So what is caching? Well, we know it. Caching is to reduce the number of calls made into the backend. So that means that our clients, when they talk to the API gateway, the API gateway will first check the cache and if a result is already in cache, return that result. Otherwise, if there's a cache miss, then it will go and talk to the backend to get the response.

So the idea is that we really leverage a lot of the cache to reduce the amount of pressure on our backend. So the default TTL, which is how long the results live in the cache is 300 seconds. So five minutes, but the min is zero, that means no caching and the max is one hour. The caches are defined at the stage level. So you define one cache per stage, and it is possible for you to override the cache settings per method. So if you want a method to not use a cache, you can specify it as well at the method level.

The cache can be encrypted and the cache size is between 0.5 gigabytes, all the way to 237 gigabytes. The cache is really expensive, so it makes sense only if you're in production but it may not make sense if you're in development or test environment, for example, because there's not that many requests done on your backend anyway. So caching is really something you wanna use in production or in pre-production. Now, how do we invalidate the cache?

So you are able to invalidate the entire cache immediately from the UI, or clients can invalidate the cache with the header placed into a query to the API gateway called Cache-Control:max-age equals zero. And for the clients to do this, they need proper IAM authorization. So this is an IAM policy that would allow a client to invalidate the cache on a specific resource. And if you don't impose an InvalidateCache policy or if you don't require authorization in the console, then any clients can invalidate the API cache and that could be a disaster.

So now you know everything about caching. Let's go in the hands-on to see how that works. So let's practice caching on our API. For this, let's go to the prod stage and edit the stage details. And here we have the cache setting. So we're going to enable it but this is not part of the features. So if you wanna follow along, just know that you'll have some charges. So you can choose the cache capacity. If you have many different API calls to cache, of course, you want a bigger one.

Do you want to encrypt the cache data or not? And what is the cache TTL? So how long should the record live in your cache? 300 seconds is five minutes. So this is a good default but you have anything between zero and 3,600 seconds. Next, you have also a per-key cache invalidation. That means that some values of the cache can be invalidated based on the key but this could be dangerous. So you may want to require authorization to say, hey, only authorized people can actually invalidate the cache.

And if so, if it's unauthorized, what do you do? You just ignore the cache control header that was used to invalidate the cache. Or do you wanna fail with a 403 or do you wanna add a warning? And so on. So this is just some things to look at. So for example, we can require authorization and just ignore the cache control header. Okay, so let's save this. So now we have a cache on our entire API and this would work already but you can also further customize the cache and say, for example, for this GET method, you can actually override how the cache is working.

So you can edit it and say, well, there should be a per-method cache where you define a specific TTL. You can also define specific rules for the cache invalidation and so on. So let's test the cache. So it's not something you're going to be seeing necessarily but if you go to the stage and it says hello from Lambda and you refresh, now the result is coming from the cache and not from your Lambda function. So the idea here is that if people are repetitively using the same routes with the same arguments, then instead of asking every time Lambda to fetch a result, it's going to be cached in API gateway.

So that's it. You've seen how the cache is working. Now to stop incurring costs, please disable the API cache and you'll be good to go. All right, that's it. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: API Gateway Usage Plans & API Keys
lectures.text:
So we have now created our API and it is time to make it available for our customers and we may want to charge them some money for it. So for this, there is a concept of usage plans and API keys. So the way it works that we create a usage plan in which we define who can access one or more API stages and method, how much and how fast they can access them, and which API keys are linked to this usage plan to identify the clients and meter their access.

Then we can also configure throttling limits, so how fast the users can target our API, and quotas in case we just want to say, for example, that only 10,000 requests a month can be done on our API before you need to pay some more. And then we can create API keys. These are just string to distribute to your customers and they look like this. And these API keys allow your customers to securely use your API gateway and authenticate their requests.

And you can use this in conjunction with the usage plan to control access. And if you enable any throttling limits, it is applied at the API key level. Overall, the quota limit is the overall number of requests. So by using the usage plan and the API keys, we're able to really monitor, offer our API and limit it for our customers. So what's the order in which you create an API key and a usage plan? So in order to configure a usage plan, you need to remember it.

You need to first create one or more API and then configure the methods that will require an API key and then deploy the API to your stages. Then you will generate or import API keys to distribute to your application developers, so they're your customers who will be using your API. And then you create a usage plan with the desired throttle and quota limits. And finally, you need to associate the API stages and API keys with the usage plan. And the last step, if you forget it, then things will not work.

Finally, the callers of the API must supply an API key in the XAPI key header request into the API. So that's it. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: API Gateway Monitoring, Logging and Tracing
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about API Gateway Logging and Tracing. So the first option is to use CloudWatch Logs. And when you enable CloudWatch log integration with API Gateway, you're going to get information about the request and the response body that goes through the API gateway. You can enable it at the Stage Level and you define your Log Level, if you want to have the ERROR logs only, or DEBUG, or INFO. And obviously the DEBUG is going to give you the most amount of information, and you can override this setting on a per API basis.

So to make it dead clear, we're going to get a user that makes a request into the API gateway, and automatically that request is going to be logged into CloudWatch Logs. Then the request is making it to your backend, your backend will then give a response to the API gateway, and the response again, will be sent to CloudWatch Logs and finally, make it to the user. So it's very helpful to get the request and the response, but be careful if you do enable this, then you may get a lot of sensitive information into CloudWatch Logs.

For X-Ray, well, this is to get tracing information about the requests that go through the API gateway. And if you enable X-Ray for API gateway and Lambda, that gives you of course the full picture, for your API. Then API gateway can be monitored with CloudWatch Metrics and their per stage, and you can enable detail metrics. And so there's a few metrics you need to know about, before going to go in the exam. The first one is called CacheHitCount, and the other one is called CacheMissCount, which gives you some information about the efficiency of your cache.

So if your cache is very efficient, the cache hit will be very high. If it's not efficient, the cache miss will be very high. The count is a number of API requests in a given period. The IntegrationLatency is how long the API takes to relay a request to the backend, and waiting for receiving a response from the backend, so it indicates to you, how long the backend is taking to reply to the API gateway. And the Latency itself, is the time between when the API gateway receives a request from the client, and when it returns a response to the client.

So that includes the IntegrationLatency, but also adds anything the API gateway is doing. That includes, for example, checking the authorization and authentication, checking the cache, doing some mapping templates, and so on. So the Latency is always going to be a bit higher than the IntegrationLatency. And so you should note, that the maximum amount of time that an API gateway can perform any request is 29 seconds. So if your Latency or your IntegrationLatency is over 29 seconds, that means you will see a timeout from your API gateway.

So this is two, these are two really good metrics to look at. Then we have two kinds of errors. So we're getting some metrics related to these errors. You have a 4XX metric, called client-side errors. So this is how many errors we're getting on the client side. And 5XXError which is how many errors we're getting on the server side. So server-side means backend, and client-side means the clients using your API gateway. Okay, so we've seen the API gateway can do some throttling with the usage plans and so on.

So we can define also Account Limits, And by default your API gateway will throttle requests at 10,000 requests per second, across all the API's, such as a soft limit and can be increased upon request. So that means that if one of your API is under heavy use the other APIs can also be throttled. So in case you see a throttling, what will you see? You will see an error code, 429 Too Many Requests which is a clients error, because the clients are doing too many requests, and it's retriable but you should use something like exponential back off, to retry these requests.

You can also, to improve throttling and performance set stage limits and method limits to make sure that each stage does not use all the quotas of the request, if it's under attack. Or, we've seen before we can define a usage plan, if we want to be able to throttle, per customer. So just like Lambda Concurrency, if one API is overloaded, if not limited, it can cause other APIs to be throttled. So we've seen this with Lambda Reserve Concurrency and concurrency overall but this is also applicable to API Gateway.

Okay, finally, let's talk about the errors we can see in the API gateway. So 4xx means Client errors, So the clients using your API Gateway. This could be 400:Bad Request 403:Access Denied, or the web application firewall did not accept your request. 429, for example, if your quota has been exceeded and you're seeing some throttling. And anything with 5XX, means Server errors, so your backend. So 502 means that for example, your Lambda proxy integration did not respond well, or 503 is that your backend is unavailable.

Or 504 is that there was an Integration Failure, and one of these failures is that the API gateway did request timeout and after 29 seconds did not receive a request from the backend and therefore we returned a 504:Integration Failure, due to this timeout. So that's it for the API Gateway Monitoring. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: API Gateway CORS
lectures.text:
So, API Gateway supports the browser security cross-origin resource sharing. So, CORS must be enabled if you want to be able to receive API calls from another domain. So for this, API gateway works without and we create an OPTIONS pre-flight request and then, this contain the following CORS headers. Access-Control-Allow-Methods, Access-Control-Allow-Headers, allow origins, and so, these methods can be set from the console. And so, to summarize how CORS are and how they work, here is a very concrete example.

So, our web browser goes to our S3 bucket to get our static website content which is at example.com, ww.example.com. And the JavaScript that we've launched and launched from the S3 bucket is asking us to make API calls into our cross-origin api.example.com. So as such, our web browser as a security, will make an OPTIONS pre-flight request into our API gateway. Then, our API gateway will give us a pre-flight response if the origin is allowed to make a cross-origin request.

And finally, if everything goes well, then the web browser and the API gateway can talk to one another. So from an exam perspective, all you need to know is that CORS can be enabled on the API gateway in case you're doing cross-origin types of requests. All right, that's it. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: API Gateway Authentication and Authorization
lectures.text:
Now here is a pretty heavy lecture around API gateway security, but one you should master, so I've tried to include as many diagrams as possible. So the first one is to use IAM permissions to access your API gateway. That makes sense, this is what we've been doing so far, we use an IAM policy and we attach it to user enroll and we're able to invoke our API gateway. So in this case the authentication is done through IAM and the authorization is done through an IAM policy.

So this is the optimal way to protect your API gateway if it's being accessed within your AWS accounts, so that includes if you're using EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or IAM users, et cetera et cetera. In order to pass your IAM credentials to the API gateway, there is a leverage of the signature before capability where the eight credentials are going to be signed and then placed into headers. So let's take an example, the API gateway is deployed into a stage and secured with IAM permissions, and there's a backend of Lambda functions.

So first our clients is going to do a rest API call and we'll pass the Sig v4 headers, then API gateway knows how to decrypt those, so it will check with IAM if the user is authorized and so there will be an IAM policy check, and so as soon as this is done the API gateway will, if it's authorized, talk to the Lambda function in the backend and returned a result to the clients. So there's is a first permission mode and it is very simple. Now this can be combined with resource policies.

So, resource policies sound a lot like Lambda resource policies because they are for the exact same purpose, they allow you to set adjacent policy on your API gateway to define who and what can access your API gateway. So the main use case of resource policies is to use cross account access, so we would define adjacent policy just like this and combined it with IAM security, we are able to give access of users or roles in other accounts directly into our API gateway.

So this is for cross account access, but you could also use resource policy to filter for specific IP addresses, or to allow only for a VPC Endpoint. So there is the first category of security. The second category is around Cognito user pool, so we'll see Cognito in its own section, but Cognito at a high level It's a database of users. So Cognito will manage fully the user lifecycle and the token of connection to Cognito will expire automatically, and so the API Gateway will verify the identity of the people connecting to API with Cognito.

There's no custom implementation required, so in this case the users have to authenticate with the Cognito User Pools, and then the authorization is set at the API gateway methods level. So, if we have a look here our API gateway is talking to Lambda function in our backend, and then, our client first authenticates with the Cognito User Pool to retrieve a connection token. So the users are already restarting user pool, then our client is authenticated they received a token and it will pass the token in the API call to our API gateway.

Now what will happen is that the API gateway has a direct integration with Cognito User Pools, and it will evaluate the Cognito token with the Cognito User Pool and if the token is correct, it's going to allow access to your backend. So this is a very easy kind of security one will be exploring. And then the last one is Lambda Authorizer, formerly called Custom Authorizer, and this one is the most flexible but requires the most involvement on your end.

So it is a Token-based authorizer with a bearer token, and this looks like a JWT so JSON Web token or Oauth. And so the idea is that, we can pass a request based parameters with headers or query strings into a Lambda authorizer, and the Lambda function will have to evaluate what we passed to it, and if it's happy, return an IAM policy for the clients that made the request and the policy will be cached. So I will be explaining this in diagram it will be much clearer.

So the authentication in this time is external so it's up to you to authenticate users any where you want, and the authorization has to be done in your Lambda function. So, here's a diagram it should make a lot more sense. So the API gateway has a backend to get on the function, and our clients first authenticates with a third party authentication system. For example, it could be off zero. lectures.title: API Gateway Websocket API
lectures.text:
So let's discuss, WebSocket APIs with API gateway. So what is WebSockets? WebSocket, anytime you see it, it means that there is a two way interactive communication between the user's browser and a server. And it's two-way because the server, it can choose to push back information to the client without having the clients making a request to the server, okay? So this enables stateful application use cases. And so WebSocket APIs are often going to be used in real time applications such as chat applications, collaboration platforms, multiplayer games and financial trading platforms.

So in the context of a chat application, the client is going to connect to a WebSocket API on API gateway and is going to establish a persistent connection. So there's not multiple connections, it's just our connection is open and the API gateway is connected to the clients. Then on the first connection there's going to be a Lambda function called onConnect. There's going to be invoked and you can do whatever you want such as persisting the connection ID into DynamoDB and we'll see this in details in the next slides.

Then whenever the client chooses to send a message over this persistent connection, it can invoke a new Lambda function called sendMessage. And then finally, when the client has sent many messages and want to disconnect, you will be sending a message to the Lambda function, onDisconnect. So we can work with any kind of integration API gateway has in the backend. It could be Lambda functions, it could be DynamoDB tables, or HTTP endpoints or whatever you want, okay?

The idea is that there's a WebSocket API. So what I'm not showing in this graph is how to send data back to the clients. But I will be showing this to you right now in the slides as we go over the details over how WebSockets works because I think it is important to you to understand this, to understand the questions of the exam. So there's a WebSocket URL that start with wss, it's an encrypted WebSocket URL. And it looks like there's some unique ID, .execute-api.region.amazonaws.com/the stage name.

So this is when you deployed your WebSocket API. So the client is going to connect to your WebSocket API gateway and establish a persistent connection into it which is going to invoke the Lambda function and perform a connection ID. And the connection ID is going to remain persistent as long as the client is connected to the API gateway. Then the connection ID can be for example, persistent into Amazon DynamoDB to store some metadata around the, what, who the user is for example.

Then the client wants to send some messages to the server. So is going to use the same URL I just gave you, some dummy data in here. And is going to send messages over the persistent connection into the WebSocket API and these messages are called frames. So these frames are going to invoke a new Lambda function and we'll see how the routing works in a few minutes. But the connection ID is going to be the same. So the Lambda function can interact with DynamoDB to retrieve the user information based on the connection ID, do whatever it wants and maybe persist some messages back into DynamoDB.

And so if the clients chooses to send more messages through the API gateway on the WebSocket API, is just going to send it more frames over the same connection. And therefore the connection ID is not going to change and it's going to be reused when the Lambda function is invoked. Now, how does the server, our API gateway communicate back to the clients without the client making a request? So again, we use the same WebSocket URL and we do the same thing as sending messages but now we want to get some data back.

And there is when you have a API gateway, a connection URL callback and it looks like this, it looks just like the URL but slash adds connections, /connectionid. And if a Lambda function or whatever, makes an HTTP post that is signed using IAM Sig v4, to this connection URL callback by specifying the connection ID of the clients, it is going to send back a message from the API gateway into the client. And this allows for two way communication which explains how you can obviously set up a chat application because you can choose send messages but also receive messages.

Now, for the operations of this URL, the very specific, /connectionsid URL you can do a post to send back a message from the server to the connected WebSocket clients. You can do a GET to get the latest connection status of the connected WebSocket clients and DELETE if you want it to disconnect the client from the WebSocket connection. Finally, how does the client know which Lambda function to invoke or which backend to invoke? In WebSocket, there's a concept of routing.

So the incoming JSON messages are going to be routed to a different backend. And if you don't specify your route, it's going to be sent to the default route. So you can select, you can create a route selection expression to select the field on the JSON to route from. So let's go through a concrete example. So say we, the incoming data from the clients into our API looks like this, the service is chat, the action is join and the data is room, room1234.

Then we have a Route Key Table that we define at the API gateway level. Where we define connect, disconnect, default which are mandatory routes and then our customer routes:join, quit, delete, et cetera, et cetera. If we specify the sample expression to API gateway, $request.body.action, it is going to look at the action field of the incoming data which currently says join. So the result of this expression is going to be evaluated against the Route Key Table available in the API gateway.

And we see that the join route does exist. And so therefore the API gateway knows that this route is connected to a specific backend and that could be a Lambda function or anything else that API gateway integrates with. And in case there is no route being matched then it's going to go into the default route. So that's it for how WebSocket APIs work. I give you way more information than what you need going into the exam but I think it is very important for you to understand how this works at a high level.

And so from an exam perspective, just remember WebSocket APIs is for two-way communication and the routing you need to understand it. The routing is used to make sure that you can route to a specific backend based on the routing expression because the connection is already open and the routing should be part of the incoming data message. So that's it. I hope this helps and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Introduction to CICD in AWS
lectures.text:
Okay, elcome to one of my favorite sections on AWS, which is the CICD section. Why? Because as a developer, CICD is so important, and that section is actually really key at the exam. So using before all the course resources, we've learned how to create AWS resources, manually we show the fundamentals, we learn how to interact with AWS programmatically, so that was using the CLI, and we learned how to deploy code to AWS using Beanstalk. But all those steps that were done here were very manual and it's very likely for us to do mistakes if we keep on doing things manually.

So what we want to do end of the day is to push our code in a target repository, and then from that code, we want it to be deployed in a automatic way onto AWS. So automatically, the right way, making sure that all code is going to be tested before it's being deployed with the possibility to go into different stages. For example, our development environment, our test environment, our staging, which is pre-prod and prod environment. And sometimes even when you want to deploy your prod, maybe you want to have manual approvals.

And so we want all these things. So we need to learn AWS CICD, and these are very important steps because we are going to automate all these steps and this is super important. So what is CIDD? So first, CICD is about continuous integration, and that means that the developers are going to push the code very often into a central code repository. And so that could be GitHub, which is a third party service from AWS, or CodeCommit, which is its AWS service, or Bitbucket, which is also a third party service.

So developers push the code to code repo, and then there's going to be a test or build server that will check if the code is correct and working as soon as it's pushed into the code repository. So this could be CodeBuild if it's AWS or Jenkins, if you want an open source tool, for example. So the build server is going to fetch a code and test it, and then as a developer, we're going to get feedback as to whether or not the test or checks will have passed or failed.

And so we get the build and test results, but we've saved time. So with this, we find bug early and we fix them early because we are testing the code as soon as it is pushed in a code repository. So the developer doesn't need to test the code on their machine, they can just push the code and wait for the build server to do it while they do some other tasks. Therefore, the code is going to be delivered faster because it's going to be tested. Thanks to this, we're gonna be able to deploy often because as soon as it's tested and ready, we can deploy it.

And then happier developers, because developers have a healthier cycle for development. So we saw CI and now there is CD, so it could be continuous delivery, for example. And so let's give you this example. So here we have application servers of version 1, and we want our code as a developer to be pushed all the way to these application servers. So the way we do it is that we've continuous delivery. Anytime we push the code onto the code repo, it's going to be deployed if it's tested appropriately onto our application servers.

So the developer pushes the code. The code is going to be tested by the build server. So this is the continuous integration part, and then after the build is passed, so it is green, so it's fully tested, then there's going to be a deployment server. And this deployment server is going to deploy our application onto our application servers. So version 1 at first. But then if we push again, a new version of our code into our code repo, then we're going to have Application Server version 2.

So with continuous delivery, we ensure that deployments happen often and that they're very quick and we shift away from a mentality of let's do one release every three months, which is very long to do, you know, error prone because it doesn't happen very often, to let's automate, you know, up to five releases a day. Because every time we push the code into the code repo, the code is going to be live on through some application servers. So to do continuous delivery, we need automated deployment tools such as CodeDeploy, which is an AWS service or Jenkins CD or Spinnaker or other tools.

So if you look at the tech stack for CICD on AWS, we have the code, and the code can live in CodeCommit or GitHub or Bitbucket or any third party code repository. Then we have build phase, the build phase, and the test phase could be done by CodeBuild on AWS, but there's a competitor to CodeBuild, which is open source called Jenkins CID or any third party CI server will do as well. Then we'll go to the deploy phase, then we can use CodeDeploy, and CodeDeploy will seek and deploy to EC2 instances, on-premises servers, Lambda functions, and ECS.

Or if you wanted to also provision the infrastructure, we could use Elastic Beanstalk as an alternative to CodeDeploy, to do the deployment and provision of the infrastructure. And then to orchestrate all these things, to define exactly what happens in our CIDCD process, then we can orchestrate everything using AWS CodePipeline. So that's it for an overview of CICD. Now in this section, we're going to do a deep dive, obviously on the AWS services, but hopefully you know the context of what we're trying to do.

Now let's go ahead and do a deep dive on all these services. So I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CodeCommit Overview
lectures.text:
So let's talk about AWS code commit now. So the concept we need to introduce is version control. It's the ability to understand the various changes that happen to code over time and possibly roll back. So to have version control, that means that you can see what happened in the past, who committed some code, what changed, what was added was removed and so on, and then roll back. And so to get version control, there is an underlying technology that's very, very popular nowadays called Git, and a Git repository can be synchronized on your computer, but it's also very usually uploaded onto a central online repository.

And the benefits of having a central online repo for a git repo is that you can collaborate with other developers. So it allows, you know, organizations up to maybe hundreds of thousands developers to work on the same code at the same time, which is amazing. Make sure that also the code is backed up somewhere. So the code lives on the cloud and not on just someone's computer, make sure it's fully viewable and editable so we can see who committed to what line of code when, and we can revert them.

You can roll back. You can do a lot of good things with code repositories And so with Code Commit, well, we have a code repository in AWS and our developers. For example, Emma and John can collaborate and push and pull code from our code repo So why do we want to use Code Commit? Well, Git repository can be quite expensive. And so there is like some industry, that offer, third party services, which is github,Gitlab, Bitbucket and so on, but the bill could be pretty high, but by using code commits, which is on AWS, you get a private git repository that's because your code actually lives and stays within your VPC on AWS cloud.

There's no size limit on the repo. That means that you can scale to, you know, gigabytes of code, if you want it to it's fully managed is highly available. And the Code, as I said, is only in the AWS cloud. So that means there is increased security and compliance, and maybe for example, unacceptable for you to have your code elsewhere then on AWS also could commit a security. So it's encrypted, you have access control using IAM and so on, and you have integrations within code commit and industry standards for such as Jenkins or CodeBuild or other CI tools, which make it a great choice to store your code.

If you want it to now Code Commit as very, very good security. So interactions are done using this standard Git command line, but then you have authentication on top of it. It could be using SSH keys. In which case, as a user, you can configure your SSH keys to be able to go into a Git repo or HTTPS. If you wanted to get access using standard login and password to get repo. for authorization, you have IAM policies are used to manage users and roles permissions to the specific repos, which is nice because that means you only have one way of managing security in AWS Encryption.

So your code is ultimately going to be encrypted using KMS. And that means that no one else, but you can retrieve it. And also while you push your code to code commit, you have encryption in transit because you use HTTPS or SSH protocols, which are both secure. And then in case of cross account access, of course you would not share you as SSH keys or your credentials with someone else. Instead, you would create an IAM role in your accounts and then use STS the AssumeRoleAPI to get access to a code commit repo.

So just to finish your high-level overview, because you may be very well familiar with GitHub. So CodeCommit versus Github is almost a one-to-one comparison in some ways, but so codecommit and Github support code reuse also called pull requests. There is both integration with code build and there is a authentication with SSL and HTTPS for both codecommit and Github. In terms of security. Now it's very different. So Github support to Github users and SSO if you have enterprise level, but codecommit is fully integrated with AWS.

So you have IAM users and roles for hosting while your code is only on AWS for codecommit, whereas Github, you can host dates directly on GitHub itself, or if you'll get an enterprise, you can host it on your own servers. The UI for codecommit, may I say is quite minimal. Whereas I really like GitHub UI it's fully featured, but again, if you're just using it as a code repo, then maybe you want to go towards code commit for many reasons that I've just said it from before. Okay.

So that's it for an overview of codecommit. I hope you liked it. And I will see you in the next lecture for some practice.

lectures.title: CodePipeline Overview
lectures.text:
Okay, so now let's talk about CodePipeline, which is a visual workflow tool that will allow you to orchestrate your CI/CD within AWS. So with CodePipeline, you can show sources such as hey, my code is in CodeCommit or we have a Docker image in ECR, or my code is in Amazon S3. Or even external tools such as Bitbucket or GitHub. Then you can move on to the build phase, which is, hey, now that we have this code, let's build it. So CodeBuild, Jenkins, CloudBees, TeamCity are all options.

Then once you have the build phase, you can have the test phase. So again, testing your code. So CodeBuild or Device Farm if you have an app, for example, an iOS, an Android app, or any third-party tools you want. Then once the code is tested, you want to deploy it. So CodeDeploy, Beanstalk, CloudFormation, ECS, S3, all these options can be handled by CodePipeline. And Invoke to invoke a Lambda function or a step function. And then when you have all these building blocks, you can build stages.

So each stage can have sequential actions and/or parallel actions. You can do a lot of things. Here's a very simple example. Build, test, deploy onto staging, then load testing to make sure staging is doing fine. And then once the load testing is done, maybe deploy again to production. Now, there's also a way for you to define manual approval at any stage in your pipeline, really allowing you, for example, just before deploying to prod to have someone review the results of the load testing, for example, if it was there.

And make sure it says, yeah, looks good. Green light, deploy to prod. So CodePipeline really is here to orchestrate everything and it gives you a lot of flexibility thanks to all the building blocks as we'll see in the next lectures. Now, how does CodePipeline work inside? So let's assume we have a source, a build and a deploy phase. So source is CodeCommit. Build is CodeBuild, even though we haven't seen CodeBuild yet, and Deploy is CodeDeploy even though we haven't seen CodeDeploy yet.

So each pipeline can create artifacts. Artifacts is whatever is created out of the pipeline and the artifacts are going to be stored in S3 buckets to be passed onto the next stage. And this is how the next stage is going to be able to do what it needs to do. So let's do a concrete example. Developer is going to push some code into CodeCommit, right? And then CodeCommit is going to be orchestrated by CodePipeline, which is going to extract all the code and create an artifact out of it and place that artifact into an S3 bucket.

Now, when CodeBuild is invoked, the same artifacts that were extracted are going to be inputted directly into CodeBuild, and that's why CodeBuild doesn't need to have straight access into CodeCommit. Actually, it's CodePipeline that will be pushing the code to CodeBuild through Amazon S3. Then when CodeBuild is building the code, it's going to create some deployment artifacts. So these artifacts are going to be stored yet again in your S3 bucket by CodePipeline, and CodePipeline will push these artifacts yet again to CodeDeploy and CodeDeploy says hey, I have these artifacts, I need to deploy them.

Let's go ahead and deploy them. So as you can see, these stages interact with each other through Amazon S3, and this is why we have artifacts in CodePipeline. Now, some troubleshooting for CodePipeline. So if you need to have a look at all these things, for example, you need to look at like CodePipeline action or stage execution state changes, you can use CloudWatch Events, EventBridge to have a look at them. So for example, you can create events for failed pipelines, events for cancelled stages and then receive an email notification, for example.

And then if CodePipeline has a failure at a stage, you will see it visually and you can get information through the console. And if there is no way for CodePipeline to perform a specific action, for example, to invoke some code in CodeBuild or to pull the code from CodeCommit, then check the IAM service role of CodePipeline and make sure it has right IAM permissions. Also, if you need to have a look at maybe some denied API calls within your infrastructure, you can use CloudTrail, which is a service used to audit AWS API calls.

So let's say for CodePipeline, it will make a lot more sense once we go to the hands on. So I will see you in the next lecture. I hope you liked it and let's get some practice.

lectures.title: CodeBuild Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about CodeBuild. So CodeBuild allows you to take a source of code, for example, CodeCommit, Amazon S3, Bitbucket, or GitHub. And then in that source there will be some build instructions. Now from an exam perspective, you need to know the name of that file, so it's buildspec.yml, and that file needs to live at the root of your code. I will show this what it means in the hands-on. Or you can also insert these instructions manually in the console, but the best practice is use buildspec.yml and this is what the exam will test you on.

So once the application is built, the output logs can be stored into Amazon S3 and CloudWatch Logs for later analysis. You can use CloudWatch Metrics to look at the build statistics, EventBridge to detect failed builds and trigger notifications, CloudWatch Alarms in case you have too many failures for example. And then the Build Projects themselves can be, and this is a bit confusing, defined either within CodeBuild of course or also within CodePipeline.

But CodePipeline can also invoke an existing CodeBuild Build Project. So if we look at CodeBuild, what can it test? Well, if you have a Java, Ruby, Python, Go, Node.js, Android, .NET Core, PHP application, then there is a pre-built image for you to run your test in CodeBuild. And if you want to have any other environment, well you can extend a Docker image and by extending it you can test for whatever language you want. But again, this is up to you to support your own environment.

So how does CodeBuild works? Well, we have our code and in this example is in CodeCommit. So we have our source code, a bunch of files, and then there is this very important file that lives at the top of your repo, which is buildspec.yml. Now, CodeBuild is going to fetch this code and then CodeBuild itself will have to have a container. So as I said, there is going to be a build environment, so Java, Go, and so on. And this container is going to load all the source code and the buildspec.yml and is going to run all the instructions that are inserted into this buildspec.yml file.

Now to build this container, CodeBuild will pull a Docker image. So either it's prepackaged by AWS for the environments I just told you before, or you provide your own Docker image to run whatever code you need. Okay, so CodeBuild will run all the instructions from buildspec.yml, and sometimes they can be quite lengthy, so there is a feature in CodeBuild to be able to cache a bunch of files in S3 Bucket if you want to reuse some files from build to build.

Okay, this is an optimization, but there's a way for you to cache some files. This is optional though. Then all the logs are going to be into CloudWatch Logs and Amazon S3 if you enable it. And then once CodeBuild is done to build your code or even test your code, it can produce some artifacts and these artifacts will be extracted out of the container, put into an S3 bucket, and this is where you can find your final outputs of CodeBuild. So the buildspec.yml file is super important.

This is what it looks like. We'll have a look at it obviously in this course, but so some very important things, that the buildspec.yml file must be at the root of your code. So at the very, very top of your code directory. Environment allows you to define some environmental variables for the execution of buildspec.yml. So you have variables that can be plaintext or you can pull them directly from the SSM Parameter Store, or you can pull secrets directly from Secrets Manager.

This would allow you, for example, to get a password or for database and so on directly from some places that of course you wouldn't want to store these passwords in plaintext into a file like buildspec.yml. Then phases, which is actually going to define what CodeBuild is going to be doing. So it's a bunch of installs, for example, to say, hey, what comments do we wanna do to install some pre-necessary packages, and so on. Pre_build, which is the comments to execute just before the build.

Build, the actual build commands, very important. Then we have post_build, which are the finishing touches. For example, once it's built, maybe create a good zip output and so on. And then the artifacts, so which files at the Docker container should be extracted and sent into Amazon S3, there's also going to be encrypted. And finally there's this cache block to say which files, usually dependencies, are going to be cached in Amazon S3 for speeding up the future builds.

So that's it for CodeBuild, I hope you liked it, and let's go into the next lecture for some practice.
