lectures.title: CodeDeploy Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about AWS CodeDeploy. So as the name indicates, it is a deployment service that will automate application deployment. What does that mean? Well, that means you have a version one of an application running and somehow, you want to upgrade it to version two. Now where can we deploy version one and version two? Well, these application versions can be deployed either to EC2 instances, on-premises servers or Lambda functions or ECS services so three different kinds of targets because EC2 instances and on-premises servers have the same methodology.

On top of it, CodeDeploy can allow you to update an application but also rollback. So in case your deployment is not working as expected, it is failing, or there's an alarm that gets triggered, then we can automatically initiate a rollback. That makes it a very safe automated deployment. On top of it, we can control how fast we want to deploy our application. We will see this later on, but we can say one instance at a time or all at a time or HalfAtATime or blue/green.

Finally, to control how CodeDeploy works, there's a file named appspec.yml that can help define how the deployment will happen. So now, let's talk about the EC2/on-premises platform. So this allows you to deploy to EC2 instances and on-premises servers, your application, and your code. And you can perform two kind of deployments, either in-place deployments or blue/green deployments. We'll see them both to understand the difference. And to work, we must first deploy the CodeDeploy agent onto the target instances because the agent is the thing that will be performing the updates on the instances.

We can define the deployment speed so, as I said, we can have a gradual deployment. For example, we can do AllAtOnce, which will update all the instances at once, but will give us the most amount of downtime because we will be down. HalfAtATime, for example, to reduce capacity by 50% or OneAtATime, which is going to be the slowest because we take down one instance at a time and update it, but of course, it's going to give us the lowest availability impact because only one instance will be down at a time or you can define your own custom deployment speed if you wanted to.

So let's have a look at how, for example, in-place deployment works for HalfAtATime setting. So here we have the v1 running on four EC2 instances. Because we're in a HalfAtATime setting in in-place deployment, two instances are going to be taken down for maintenance. So the agent will stop the application on two instances which then are going to be upgraded again by the agent to version two. And once it is done, then the other half is going to be taken down for install and then upgrade it to version two.

And so this is the process of in-place deployment for HalfAtATime setting. What about blue/green? Well, blue/green is the idea that you have, for example, an Application Load Balancer pointing to version one and all your instances are in Auto Scaling group. What's going to happen is that we're going to create a new Auto Scaling group so this can be done either manually or automatically by CodeDeploy. And CodeDeploy is going to create as many EC2 instances in this new Auto Scaling group.

So we have v1 and v2 now running in parallel and the load balancer through some process is going to be pointing now to the v2 Auto Scaling group and the v1 will be taken down. So this is a simplified version, but at least you see the process, and it's called blue/green because new instances are taken up and the old ones are terminated. So this CodeDeploy agent I've been telling you about, it must be installed on the EC2 instances as a prerequisite.

So we have the EC2 instance, and we install the CodeDeploy agent. Now you can install it directly using some Linux commands to install any software or if you wanted to have some kind of automation. If your EC2 instances are managed using Systems Manager, then you can automate the install of CodeDeploy agent using Systems Manager. Now this EC2 instance with the CodeDeploy agent will need sufficient IAM permissions to access Amazon S3. Why? Well, because in Amazon S3 will be stored the application revision.

So when we want to update from version one to version two, then the CodeDeploy agent with the proper IAM permissions attached to the EC2 instance will download the application revision from the S3 bucket. And now you know enough for CodeDeploy and EC2 instances. Now let's see how CodeDeploy works with the Lambda platform. So CodeDeploy can help you automate traffic shift for Lambda aliases. And the idea is that you can shift from v1 to v2 under an PROD alias.

I'll show you this in a second. Now this feature is fully integrated within the SAM framework that you will see soon. And so that allows us to just use the SAM framework and internally use CodeDeploy. So how does that work for the traffic-shifting function? Well, say we have a PROD alias, okay? And we have v1 that we've deployed before and v2 that we've deployed after, and we wanna shift the traffic between the v1 version and the v2 version under the PROD alias.

So the way it works is that CodeDeploy is going to make this X vary until X equals 100%. So at first, X will be zero. So that means that all the PROD alias points to the v1 function, and then X will gradually increase until he reaches 100% so that all the traffic on the PROD alias is redirecting to the v2 function. Now we have several strategies to make X evolve. So we have linear where we grow the traffic every N minutes until 100%. So in this example, LambdaLinear10PercentEvery3Minutes, that means that every three minutes, 10% will be added.

lectures.text:
So let's get started with CodeDeploy, but first we need to go into IAM to create some roles. So, in the IAM console go underneath roles and create a role. This role's going to be for an AWS service and the service we're going to be looking for is CodeDeploy. As you can see, I have three options. I can create CodeDeploy, or for Lambda, or for ECS. But because we're doing a CodeDeploy use case right now, we'll just create a CodeDeploy EC2 service role.

So let's go ahead, create this, click on next and we'll call this one, CodeDeployServiceRoleForEC2. Okay, so now we are good with this role and the second role we need to create is a role for the EC2 instance that we'll deploy to. So let's create a role, and this one is for an EC2 instance. So it's a role for it, and we're going to have a permission that allows S3 read access. So if I just type S3, I should be good to go. The idea is that if you remember the EC2 instance will be the one pulling the code from your S3 bucket.

And so, therefore it means AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess. And that policy is a very simple JSON, which allows Get* and List* on any objects. So let's click on next, and I call this one, EC2RoleForCodeDeploy. And let's create this role. Okay, so now that the roles are created, we need to go back into CodeDeploy and get started. So first we need to create an application. So I call this one, DemoApplication. And for compute platform we have three options.

We have EC2, we have Lambda, and we have Amazon ECS. So we'll choose EC2/on-premises and let's create our application. Now, to create application we need to create a deployment group. I'm going to launch an instance and I'll call this one, DemoWebServer. And I scroll down. We have Amazon Linux, we have a t2 micro, we don't need a key pair.

And then for networking settings, we're going to create a security group that allows SSH traffic and also allows HTTP traffic. This is where our web server is going to be started. Storage is good and we don't need any EC2 user data. So let's go ahead and launch this instance. And as you can see, I have not tagged my instance yet. I've just launched it so that I will show you why tags are helpful later on. Now the next steps is to SSH into our instance.

So now that it is running, I'm going to click on connect and then EC2 instance, EC2 user and click on connect. So now I am SSH'ed into my instance. And if it doesn't work for you maybe it's because the port 22 wasn't open. And now, the next step is to actually install the CodeDeploy agents. So for this, let's go into our code under CodeDeploy, under cicd, we have the commands and we do updates. So we update the operating system. So we're gonna say, okay, no updates to do.

So back into CodeDeploy, we need to enter a service role, which is created from before. So that's perfect. Now for deployment type, we have In-place or Blue/green. And it turns out that we've seen both in the previous lecture. But for this demo we're going to use In-place. And for the environment configuration we have multiple options. Are we using Auto Scaling groups? No, we're not in this case, but we could. Are we using Amazon EC2 instances? Yes, we are.

But for now, let's just choose Amazon EC2 instances, and we need to specify a tag group. So, the tag group is going to be Environment and the value is going to be Development. And right now there is no hint at this. So, let's just refresh this page and I'm going to rename this my DevelopmentGroup and Amazon EC2 instances.

So that means that my EC2 instance from here has been picked up in this deployment group. So we are good. Do we want to install the agent with Systems Manager? No, we don't need to. Well, because we already have installed the agent ourselves, so never, is good enough. But of course, if we wanted to automate the installation of it, we could use this automation right here, using Systems Manager.

But for now, never. Now for deployment settings, we have CodeDeployDefault.AllAtOnce. So this is going to update all my instances at once but we have different strategies. We have one at a time, we have half at a time, or we can create our own deployment configuration. If we wanted to have more fine grain control. If we were using a load balancer, for example, with an Auto Scaling group, we could enable this integration but right now we don't. So let's disable it and let's create our deployment group.

So we are now ready to deploy something to our EC2 instances. So let's create a deployment and this is going to apply to my development group. And my application is stored in Amazon S3. So that is not true yet, but we need to go into Amazon S3 and actually put our application there. So I'm gonna go into my S3 console, I'm going to create a bucket and make sure you choose the same region as the region of CodeDeploy. So from it's EU-west-1 Ireland.

So I'm going to say the bucket name is Stephane-code-deploy-demo, scroll all the way down and then create this bucket. And now we need to upload some data into our buckets. So what data? Well, the application itself. So I've created a zip file called SampleApp_linux.zip and this one we'll upload. But I've also unzipped it, so we can have a look at what is going on. So let's have a look first at the index.html file. And this is a simple HTML document that contains what we will display on our website after doing the CodeDeploy deployment.

But in CodeDeploy the most important file is the appspec.yml file, which contains the instructions of CodeDeploy should do to actually deploy our distribution or application. So as we can see there's a files handle here saying that this index, that HTML file should be copied into var/www/html, which is where the html files are displayed for Apache web servers. Then we have different hooks, and as we can see in here we have a BeforeInstall to install dependencies.

Then we have a start server. So after the independencies are installed let's start server. And finally, before we want to do any update we need to stop the application. So we have a stop server script and each script is actually very simple, the script right here, so install dependencies just installs htpd. Start server starts the htpd server and stop server will stop the htpd server if it exists. Okay, so we are good to go. So now let's go ahead and back into Amazon S3.

I'm going to upload my zip file. So here I found my SampleApp_Linux.zip. I'm good to go. Let's upload it. And this was successful. So now this file has been uploaded and that's the one I'm going to be using in my CodeDeploy deployments. So here what I need is the full S3 URL to it. So let's copy the S3 URI right here and paste it. Okay? So it's a zip file as we can see, but we have other types of compression mechanism if you want. Okay, so now we're good to go.

We are not going to touch the deployment description we're not going to talk about failures, we're not going to be talking about content options or overrides. We're just going to go and create this deployment. So now the deployment has been successfully created and my progress of the lifecycle events is going to appear right here. So let's click on view events. And it's going to show you all the events that are going to happen for my ES2 instance, as you can see we're going to have ApplicationStop, DownloadBundle, BeforeInstall, Install, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart and ValidateService.

So for this, the CodeDeploy agent must pick up the fact that there is a new deployment. And my deployment just failed, and I know why. It's because I forgot to attach the instance role to my EC2 instance. So you may have noticed this while I was doing the video. Anyway, just go to action and then security, and then modify IAM role, and we'll choose the IAM role called EC2RoleForCodeDeploy. And this of course allows my EC2 instance to actually get the files from Amazon S3.

So let's try again to run a deployment. So for this, let's go into this one. I'm going to do retry deployments, and now it's started and hopefully now my EC2 instance should be able to get the file from S3, and therefore the deployment should happen. So let's view the events now. And as we can see now, my deployment has worked. So we have ApplicationStops, then DownloadBundle, BeforeInstall, Install, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart and ValidateService.

And to verify that everything has been working, Let's go to ESC2 instance. I'm going to copy the public IP and type http: and the IP address. And we have a congratulations. This application was deployed using AWS CodeDeploy. So that's it. We've performed our first deployment on CodeDeploy. Of course, you could update the application, update the S3 bundle zip, and then redeploy it. And it will be again, redeployed to your EC2 instances based on your configurations.

So to summarize, we've looked at deployments, we've looked at the applications. We can look at deployment configurations where you can see that you can deploy on EC2, on Lambda, on ECS, as well. And you can create a deployment configuration for the platform you want. So if you wanted to customize, for example, the number of healthy hosts as a percentage with a number for controlling how CodeDeploy deploys your application. And also, you can register on-premises instances here, so that CodeDeploy can deploy the application on-premises as well.

Also, please do not forget to terminate the EC2 instance you've created. All right, that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CodeDeploy for EC2 and ASG
lectures.text:
So let's have a look at a few more concepts for, CodeDeploy. So when we approach an EC2 instance, we're going to have the appspec.yml at the root of your code and then deployment strategy. So we can do, for example, in place updates to your fleet of EC2 instances, and then we can use hooks. We set them in the expert Hemel to verify the deployments after each deployment phase. So here we have a half at a time. So half of them is going to be taken down, then upgraded to version two.

The other half is going to be taken down. I've got your version two, and this is an in-place deployment. Now for ASG deployments of code, the deployment's a little bit more complicated. So we have two options. We have in-place deployments and blue/green. So in-place we'll be doing the exact same thing we saw before. It will update existing EC2 instances. And in case you create a new EC2 instances in your ASG automatically, it's going to get a deployment by CodeDeploy, which is very nice.

So this is where it could differ with ASG is very powerful. So this is for in-place deployment, but we also have blue/green deployments. And in this case, a new auto-scaling group is going to be created and settings are going to be copied. Then we get to choose how long do you keep the old EC2 instances, you old ASG. And then the ELB, that redirects from one target group to the other, is going to fall over. So let's set an example. So this is our blue/green deployments or the ELB.

We have our EC2 instances on launch template V1 within the ASG, and then CodeDeploy is going to deploy the V1 application to these EC2 instances. Now, in case we want to upgrade to version two, then new instances are going to be created. And then with launch pad V2, CodeDeploy is going to deploy the application to these EC2 instances. Then the ELB is going to receive traffic from both the V1 and V2 instances for says for a bit, then, if everything is healthy, V version one will be taken down and we will have done a blue/green deployment.

Finally, around the redeploys and rollbacks. So a rollback is when, when you want to redeploy a previously deployed revision of your application, so you want to go back in time, and deployments can be rolled back in two ways: either automatically, for example, when we have a failure of the deployment or when we have a CloudWatch Alarm that is being triggered and say, Hey the deployment has failed, or manually. If we disable rollbacks, then there will be no rollbacks performed for this deployment. Okay?

And when the rollback happens, what happens is that CodeDeploy actually redeploys the last known good revision as a new deployment, okay, it doesn't go back in time. It actually performs a new deployment with a last known good version that was known to do a good deployment. So it's not a restored version. It's definitely a new deployment, and this is something that exam may test you on. So that's it for this lecture, very theory, but I know, but it's going to be helpful for your exam.

I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CodeArtifact - Overview
lectures.text:
Okay, so now let's discuss CodeArtifact. So the idea is that when you build software, you use other software that your own software depends on. This is called code dependencies. And every time you build software it's very common to push the software into a repository, and then other software can build onto it. So there is this whole dependencies, and this whole dependencies web is called artifact management. So traditionally, when you use artifacts you set up your own artifact management system, and the idea is that it could be quite complicated.

So using CodeArtifact, you get a secure, scalable, cost-effective artifact management system for software development. And CodeArtifact has more than this. I'll show you this in the diagram, but it has integration with common dependency measuring tools such as Maven, Gradle, npm, yarn, twine, pip, and NuGet. And the idea is that using CodeArtifact, both developers and CodeBuild can retrieve the dependencies straight from CodeArtifact within your AWS cloud.

So let's do a diagram is going to be much clearer. So with CodeArtifact, all your artifacts live within your VPC, within AWS. Sometimes if you use other artifact management systems they could be third parties outside of AWS, or if you deploy your own artifact measurement system they could live on these two instances, for example. In which case, yes, of course it will be within your VPC. So with CodeArtifact, you're going to define domains, and each domain is just a set of repositories.

Now, as a developer, the cool thing is that you can tell the developers, hey, you need to, for example, for your JavaScript developers run the npm command to fetch dependencies for your JavaScript packages to CodeArtifact. And CodeArtifact is going to be a proxy for public artifact repositories. So instead of having your JavaScript developers actually directly reach into the public artifact repo themselves, they're going to reach to CodeArtifact, which is going to be wired to public artifact repositories and the request will be proxied.

Why will you do this, well for two reasons, number one, network security. So your JavaScript developers only interact with CodeArtifact, and CodeArtifact will proxy the request to the public repo. But also as the dependencies are being fetched, they're going to be cached into CodeArtifact itself. Which means that even if the dependency disappears from the public artifact repository, you will still have your own copy within CodeArtifact. Which is good to make sure that your code can always be built in the future.

Now this works for not just JavaScript, but also for Python with pip. It works for .net with NuGet and Java with Maven. Okay? So all these things can be proxied from CodeArtifact into this own repositories. But the second thing you can do is obviously push your own artifacts. And so your IT leader or your developers can publish and approve packages to be pushed into other repositories within CodeArtifact. That means that all your artifacts will live in one place in your VPC.

And everything will just depend on everything, all the code that's already within your CodeArtifact, artifact management system. And if developers can get all these artifacts out of CodeArtifact, then of course CodeBuild can also too. And it is that now CodeBuild instead of fetching from public repositories, can also fetch all this information directly from CodeArtifact. Next, how does CodeArtifact changes trigger some stuff downstream in AWS? So we will see this service in detail later on, but CodeArtifact events such as when a package is created or modified or deleted will emit events into what's called EventBridge.

And EventBridge is like a repository of events within AWS. And from EventBridge, you can pretty much integrate and trigger many different AWS services, such as Lambda functions, Step functions, SNS, SQS. And if none of these terms mean anything to you by now, that's okay. We will see these later on in this course. And also, for example, CodePipeline. So it is possible for CodeArtifact to trigger CodePipeline through EventBridge, whenever a package version for example is updated.

And so why would we wanna do this? Well, for example, CodePipeline could have CodeCommit so that we know that the dependency has been updated. Then triggering CodeBuild to rebuild your application with the updated dependency maybe for security reasons. And then finally deploy the new application to your production environment using CodeDeploy. So this could be a nice automated way to build a full automated pipeline that ensures that you always have the latest dependencies in your code within your builds.

So any artifact repository within your accounts can be easily accessed by your users of your accounts or your roles with your accounts with an IAM policy. But if you want to authorize another account, and users and roles of that account to access CodeArtifact then you need to use a resource policy. So when you grant someone access to a CodeArtifact repository, what's going to happen is that you either give them access to all packages or none of them.

You cannot say only access these packages. So when you authorize another account to access your repo you authorize, for example, Bob in Account B to access all packages within that specific repo. And to give access to Bob to your accounts, what you can do is use a resource policy in which you authorize, for example, Bob of the other accounts to read the packages in your code artifact repo. And this cannot be done without a resource policy but it's just something you need to know for one question at the exam.

But this is a recurring topic in AWS. Whenever you need cross account access sometimes, most of the times, resource policies are going to be the way to go. Okay, so that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: SAM Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about AWS SAM. So SAM is this little squirrel, but it's also the Serverless Application Model. It's an actual framework to develop and deploy serverless applications. So that means that you write your code and then you're going to use a configuration in the YAML format, which is going to be compliant with the SAM framework. And automatically, SAM is going to generate very complex CloudFormation files from simple SAM YAML files.

It supports anything from CloudFormation. So you can still use outputs, mappings, parameter, resources, et cetera in your SAM YAML code. Now, SAM behind the scene can also use CodeDeploy to deploy Lambda functions, and SAM can help you run Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB locally. So SAM really is intended to be focused on serverless applications and allow you to debug them locally and to deploy them very quickly using CloudFormation into the AWS cloud.

So SAM is made of recipes, and at the very top of your template, you're going to add a transform header to indicate it's a SAM template. And this is a transform header which is going to tell CloudFormation to transform it into a CloudFormation template. Then you write your code, but instead of using the CloudFormation constructs, you're going to use the SAM constructs, such as a serverless function, which is a Lambda function, a serverless API, which is going to be the API gateway, and the serverless SimpleTable, which is going to be DynamoDB.

But you have these constructs to make it simpler and easier for you to write your serverless applications. And then to package and deploy this application onto AWS, you're going to use the sam deploy command. And it used to be two commands. It used to be sam package and then sam deploy. But now you can just do sam deploy on its own, and it is going to package it for you as well. There's also a way to synchronize your changes into AWS Lambda very quickly using SAM Accelerate, and the command is sam sync and then minus minus watch.

I'll give you a bit more information on this in this lecture. So let's have a look into SAM deployment. So you have your application code as well as your SAM template in the YAML format, and then you're going to build the application locally using sam build. It's going to transform into a CloudFormation template and your application code, and then you can deploy it using sam deploy. So you'll zip and upload everything into an S3 bucket, and then automatically execute or ChangeSet against CloudFormation.

Then your CloudFormation stack can be made of different serverless components such as Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB. So let's talk about SAM Accelerate. So SAM Accelerate is its set of features that is used to reduce the latency while deploying resources to AWS. So you want to deploy as fast as possible. And the command is going to be sam sync to declare your project, declare it with a SAM template into AWS. And it's actually going to bypass CloudFormation if you just do code changes without updating your infrastructure by using the service API.

So it's going to be a very, very quick deployment. So you have SAM template and your application code, and your Lambda function already deployed and you're going to run sam sync. And automatically, as you change the application code, automatically SAM is going to synchronize its code with your Lambda function. Therefore, if you wanted to test your Lambda function in the cloud, it's going to be very easy and very quick. So different options, you can just run sam sync to synchronize the code and the infrastructure, or sam sync and just the code option to synchronize only the code and not the infrastructure.

So you're not going to use CloudFormation, it's going to be like the updates will be done in seconds. Then you can specify a specific resource to say, hey, I only want to update my Lambda functions and their dependencies, or I want to update this specific Lambda function using the resource ID. Or you can use the watch option, which is going to monitor for file changes. So it's going to run in the background and automatically synchronize anything when changes are detected.

So if you include configuration, use sam sync, or if it's just a code, then it's going to be using sam sync and then the code option. So I hope that makes sense. I hope this is a good overview of SAM. We'll do some hands-on to practice as well so it becomes clear for you how it works. So I hope you like this lecture and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: SAM Policy Templates
lectures.text:
So let's talk about SAM policy templates or serverless model policy templates because they can come up in the exam as well. So it's a list of templates that you can apply permissions to your Lambda functions. And so, they're very simple templates and they allow you to reason much easily about what your Lambda function can do based on these templates that regroup a set of permissions. There's a full list of all the SAM policy templates that are available at this link and there's a lot of them, but I wanna walk you through three important examples.

Overall, it's pretty self explicit about what they do once you see them once. So for example, if we have S3ReadPolicy, this is a policy template that gives read only permissions to objects in S3. That makes sense, right? SQLPollerPolicy allows your Lambda function to poll an SQS queue. And DynamoDBCrud, C-R-U-D, Policy. C-R-U-D in this case means create read update delete. So that means that you are able, from your Lambda function, to do create, update, delete, and read operations to your DynamoDB table.

Overall, it's pretty self explicit, but once you see how it's defined it makes a lot of sense. So for example, say we define a function. It's running Python 2.7 and we want to be able to read from SQS. In this case, instead of attaching an I-A-M role what we do is that we create a SQS. We call the policy SQSPollerPolicies in this little orange box right here and say okay we wanna be able to poll this queue name and automatically when the SAM policy template has been transformed by the SAM framework, it will become IAM policy attached to our Lambda function.

The idea with the SAM policy templates is that it becomes much easier to write what your function should do and prevents you from worrying too much about how you should provide, er provision, your IAM roles. Okay, so that's it. All you should know for SAM policy templates. Make sure you just see once how they look like so on the right hand side and from the name of the policy template usually it's pretty obvious what they do. All right. Well, that's it.

Thank you so much for watching. I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: SAM - Local Capabilities
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about the local capabilities of the SAM framework. So by using the SAM framework, you can actually locally start AWS Lambda. So if you do SAM local start-Lambda, you will have your Lambda function available as a local endpoint on your computer with an emulation of the Lambda framework. The beautiful thing about it is that now you can start to run automated tests against these local endpoints. You can also locally invoke a Lambda function.

For this, you do SAM local invoke and this will actually invoke Lambda function with a payload. So you will do it once and then quit after the invocation is complete. It's very helpful to generate test cases and in case your Lambda function is interacting with AWS because, for example, you're doing a API call to DynamoDB to fetch whatever, re whatever thing from it, then, of course, you must start your local function or invocate with the correct --profile option because you need to say against which environment you want to be running against.

You can also start a local API Gateway Endpoint. For this you do SAM local start-API and it's going to start a local HTTP server that will host all your APIs and all your functions. lectures.title: SAM - Multiple Environments
lectures.text:
So SAM allows you as well to easily manage multiple environments within your development stack. So imagine that you're deploying sometimes your SAM templates into a dev environment and sometimes into a prod environment. So you as a developer, you have your SAM templates, but you're also going to create another file named "SAMconfig.toml". And this file looks like this. So it's in the TOML formats, and you actually have different parameters for different stacks.

So here we have the dev stack, and we define the deploy parameter. So we type, we give a stack name, we give an S3 bucket, prefix, a region, some capabilities, and parameter overrides to say, hey, the environment is development. We can also set the sync parameters the same way. And similarly, we can set the prod deploy parameters by just starting by prod.deploy.parameters, and again define the stack name, the S3 bucket, the region, and so on. And this time for the parameter overrides, we say, hey, the environment is production.

And we can also specify some sync parameters. So the reason why we do this is that once we have done this initial setup in your TOML file, then you can do "sam deploy", and then "--config-env dev". And automatically the SAM CLI is going to look into your "Samconfig.toml" file, is going to pick up the correct parameters and automatically deploy resources to the correct environment and the correct places. And of course, you can change your command to say, "sam deploy --config-env prod", and you can define of course, as many environments as you need.

So that's it. It's something that can come up in the exam. So I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CDK Overview
lectures.text:
Now let's talk about the AWS Cloud Development Kit, or CDK, which allows you to define your cloud infrastructure in a familiar programming language, such as JavaScript or TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET. So you may be saying, "Hey, it looks like this is overlapping with CloudFormation, because CloudFormation we can define the cloud infrastructure using YAML. But now we can do it using a programming language. So what is this?" Well, this is something that supersedes CloudFormation, as we'll see in a second.

So let's say we want to define our infrastructure using TypeScript, and so we have this code right here in which we are defining three different things. We are defining constructs, and so there are high level components that we can use thanks to the CDK. So the first construct we're using is a VPC. So we create a new VPC, we give it a name, and we give it three AZs. And this creates a VPC for us which is going to contain some pre-made configuration.

Then we define an ECS cluster. And the ECS cluster is named MyCluster and has a link to the VPC we just defined. And then we define an application load-balanced Fargate service, so this is a Fargate service with an ALB which is linked to the cluster we just defined. We define how much CPU, how many tasks we want, so six, the task image options, the memory limits, and that we want a public ALB. So all of this is defined using a programming language, which means that if we don't have functioning code if the code doesn't compile, then it's going to give us an error, and that means that our template cannot be generated.

But if the code can be compiled because it is sound and typesafe, then it is going to be compiled into a CloudFormation template. It could be either JSON and YAML. And so therefore, we are using the CDK to define CloudFormation templates in the backend. But this is allowing us to be a lot more flexible about it and use a programming language. So that also means that we can deploy infrastructure and application runtime code together. So this is great for Lambda functions, great for Docker containers in ECS or EKS.

So this is a revolution because CloudFormation template is YAML, it's not typesafe, you can make errors, and you only know at the very end if it worked or not. But with the CDK, you can define those using constructs and a programming language. So if you want a diagram, then we have our application constructs. It could be Lambda functions, DynamoDB, Amazon S3, ECS, some step functions, and so on. And we can use programming languages, such as Python, TypeScript, Java, .NET.

We write our CDK file, I guess, and then we synthesize this using the CDK CLI into a CloudFormation template that we will apply into CloudFormation to define our infrastructure. So it is a step above CloudFormation and makes it way easier to work with CloudFormation. So you may ask me, what is the difference between CDK and SAM? Well, SAM is going to be serverless focused, and we are going to write our templates declaratively in JSON or YAML, and this is great for quickly getting started with Lambda.

It also leverages CloudFormation in the backend, okay? But the focus of SAM is Lambda function and serverless applications. For the CDK, well, it is a super set of CloudFormation, so this supports every AWS services out there. And you're going to write your infrastructure with a programming language you know, for example, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET And it also leverages CloudFormation because it generates CloudFormation. So hopefully the difference is clear between these two services.

There's also a way where you can combine the CDK and the SAM framework. So you can use the SAM CLI to locally test your CDK applications. How? Well, first we must run cdk synth, and when we do that, we have a Lambda function say, in the CDK application, we run the cdk synth command and this is going to generate a CloudFormation template that has been synthesized from the CDK. But then, thanks to this CloudFormation template, we can use the same framework and do SAM local invoke reference the CloudFormation template and call the function.

And these two frameworks work really well together. So in the next lecture, we're going to do a hands-on on CDK. And with this hands-on, we're going to deploy an application that allows us to deploy an S3 bucket on which the users can put an image. This S3 bucket is going to trigger a Lambda function which is going to send an API call to Rekognition to analyze the image and get the results back from Rekognition, and then the Lambda function is going to save the results to Amazon DynamoDB.

And all of this is going to define all from within a CDK script. So let's go and do this in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CDK - Constructs
lectures.text:
So Constructs in CDK are very important, and we've seen them before. They are components that encapsulates everything CDK needs to create the final CloudFormation stack. And so a Construct can be a single AWS resource, such as an S3 bucket, or it can be a combination of multiple related resources, for example, an SQS worker queue with some computes. So how do we get these Constructs? Well, there is a Construct Library, which is a collection of Constructs that is included in the CDK and that contains the Constructs for every AWS resource.

And you have three levels of Constructs: Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3. We'll see them in the next slides. Also, you have the Construct Hub. This is when you have Constructs from AWS but also third parties and open-source CDK community to allow you to create your CDK stacks faster and better. So let's talk about the Layer 1 Constructs. They're called CFN Resources because they represent all the resources available within CloudFormation. So here, in this example, we do a bucket.

And it's new s3.CfnBucket. And so we define the exact same properties as the one from the CloudFormation Resource Specifications. And you know this is Layer 1 because it starts with Cfn. So a CFN bucket must have all the resource properties that are required for a bucket. So, bucket name. And you can configure all of them individually. So if you wanted to just migrate from CloudFormation to CDK, one by one, all your resources into code, you could use CFN bucket, CFN SQS queue, and so on.

And that would be enough. But that would be using Layer 1 of CDK because this is quite basic. Then you go into Layer 2. So Layer 2 is AWS resources but with a higher level. Because now we talk about intent. This is a higher level Construct. So if we have a look at what's in bottom, here we have an s3.Bucket. So the difference is that it doesn't start with Cfn. And then, as we can see, we have versioned: true. And then encryption, s3.BucketEncryption.KMS.

And then, automatically, knows how to do this. And then, out of this, from the bucket, we can get, for example, what is the HTTP URL of a specific object out of it. So we have extra methods out of it. So when you use a Layer 2 Construct, you have similar functionality as Layer 1, but now we have convenient defaults and boilerplates. So you don't need to know everything about the resource properties. And then you have added methods, such as bucket.addLifeCycleRule.

And this would allow you to just add the Lifecycle rule, even though, behind the scenes, it may be a bit more complicated in raw CloudFormation. Then you have Layer 3 Constructs. And these are called Patterns because they represent multiple related resources. So here what we have is a Lambda Rest API. And then we add resources and add resources, and do an HTTP Integration, and so on. And so, this Layer 3 Patterns will help you complete most common tasks in AWS, such as, for example, creating a Rest API with an API Gateway.

But instead of configuring every single little resource behind the scene, you have a much easier API to deal with, where you just define the API, and then you define the resources and the methods, and the Lambda functions, but very easily. You can also have, for example, an ECS pattern where you have an Application Load Balancer with a Fargate Service, which can be extremely complicated to write as raw CloudFormation. But with CDK, you just fill in the blanks, and automatically you have your ALB and your Fargate Service connected on the correct ports with the correct security groups, and so on.

And the correct listeners. So, hopefully, you now understand the differences between all the layers in CDK Constructs and the power of CDK. So I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CDK - Commands & Bootstraping
lectures.text:
Okay, so what are the important commands to know for the CDK? So you have all of these and I will walk you through them and this should make sense to you right away. So the first one is to install the CDK CLI and libraries so you can start writing your CDK stack. The second one, cdk init initializes an app from a specified template. And so you can choose Python, JavaScript and so on. Cdk synth synthesizes and prints the CloudFormation template. So this is the transformation between your CDK stack as code into a CloudFormation templates.

Cdk bootstrap is something we'll see in the next slide, so I will just skip it for now. Cdk deploy is to deploy the stack. So once you have a CloudFormation template, of course, you want to deploy it. Cdk diff is to look at the difference of the local CDK. So whatever you have changed and what is actually deployed on CloudFormation. And cdk destroy is to destroy the stacks. So the last little thing that we haven't discussed in depth is cdk bootstrap.

So what is bootstrapping in CDK? Well, bootstrapping is the process of provisioning resources for CDK before you can deploy CDK apps into an AWS environment. So what is an environment in AWS? Well, for CDK, it's the combination of an account and a region. So the idea is that before you are able to deploy to an account and a region, you must deploy a CloudFormation stack called the CDKToolkit that will contain an S3 bucket and it will contain an IAM role.

And these are necessary prerequisites to deploying any CDK stack in that specified environment. So when you are deploying to a new account and region combination, so a new environment, you do cdk bootstrap and then aws://aws_account/aws_region. So here is what happens. We have the account and the region, and the user runs the bootstrap. A CloudFormation stack called CDKToolkit is going to be created with what we need. Now, if you try to deploy a CDK stack after this, everything is going to work but if you didn't bootstrap into your environment, you will have an error when trying to deploy your CDK stack, which will say policy contains a statement with one or more invalid principle.

That's because you're missing the IAM role. So that should make sense. Hopefully now you understand what bootstrapping is and all the necessary commands to make CDK work. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CDK - Unit Testing
lectures.text:
So here is a short lecture around testing in the CDK. Well, because you are using code with CDK you can actually test your code the same way you would test normal standard Python code or JavaScript code, and so on. So in the CDK apps you have what's called the CDK assertion modules, which will contain popular test frameworks such as Jest for JavaScript or Pytest for Python. And with this assertion modules, we can verify if specific resources are what we need or rules or conditions or parameters, and so on.

So here is a simple test where we are going to have a look whether or not this synthesizes correctly. That means that the CloudFormation template that comes out of it contains what we need. So there are two types of tests in CDK. The first one is called a fine-grained assertion which is the most common, where you're going to test whether or not some specific resources have some specific properties. For example, in here we test whether or not our Lambda function has a proper handler and has a runtime of nodejs14.x.

And then we look at whether or not our SNS topic subscription is only one, okay? So this is fine-grained assertions. And then we have snapshot tests where we test the CloudFormation template against a previously stored baseline templates, for whatever reason, it's called a snapshot test. So, this is very interesting because now you can make sure that, of course, your dynamic-db table is still here with some, I don't know, common properties. Whatever you want really.

And how do we test the templates? We have two options. The first one is to do template fromStack, MyStack, and this is what we do right here where we actually import a stack that we defined in CDK and so we do templates fromStack, MyStack, but the other way is if your template does not live in CDK yet, you can do an import by doing template.fromstring. MyString in the string is your file. And the stack is going to be built outside of CDK so your CloudFormation template is outside of CDK and you can still run test against an external CloudFormation templates.

And these two commands, these two methods are very important to remember from an exam standpoint. So fromStack and fromString. All right, that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it. And I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Cognito Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about Amazon Cognito. And the goal of it is to give user an identity to interact with a web and mobile application. So these users usually sit outside of our AWS account, hence the name Cognito, because it gives an identity to users that we don't know about yet. So we have two kind of sub-services within Cognito. We have the Cognito User Pool, and this provides a sign-in functionality for app users and has really good intuition with API Gateway and the Application Load Balancer.

And we have the Cognito Identity Pool used to be called Federated Identity. And this is to actually provide temporary AWS credentials to users that are registered with our application, so that they can access some resources of AWS directly. And there is a good integration as we'll see with Cognito User Pools. So if you are asking yourself don't we already have users in IAM? The answer is yes, you do. But Cognito is gonna be for your web and mobile application users, which sits outside of AWS.

So look for the keywords such as hundreds of users or mobile users, or authentication with whatever mechanisms such as SAML and so on. Okay, that's it. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Cognito User Pools
lectures.text:
So the first surveys we will see into Cognito is called Cognito User Pools, or CUP. And, this is a way to create a serverless database for your web and mobile application users. So, what is a serverless database? That means that your users can use, for example, a simple login, their username or their email, and a password combination, to connect into your applications. They can also obviously reset their passwords, we can, thanks to Cognito User Pools, do an email and phone number verification, we can enable multi-factor authentication for our users, and we are able to tell our users they can login with Google, Facebook, or even SAML, so this is called Federated Identities.

So this is pretty much the thing you see when you go onto any other website, they ask you to register users, either create a username/password, or login Google, Facebook, or some other way. There is a feature that you can block users if their credentials are compromised elsewhere, so AWS scans the web for compromised credentials, and will let your user knows into Cognito User Pools, and then finally, and then finally, when your users log in with the Cognito User Pool, what they get back from the API is a JWT, so a JSON Web Token.

So, in a diagram, what does our Cognito User Pool look like? Well, they're a database of users, so CUP will have its own internal database of users that we can see, and then our mobile applications and our web application can login against our Cognito User Pool, and when they are logged in, the CUP will return to our user, our mobile applications and our web applications, a JSON Web Token, JWT. As I said, we can also provide login with Amazon, or Google, or Facebook, facility into our Cognito User Pools, so we can do Federation through Third Party Identity Providers, and offer a social login through a social identity provider, so login with Google, login with Facebook.

We can also integrate more specific identity providers with SAML, or even OpenID Connect, if you're identity provider supports OpenID Connect. So, that's for how CUP works at a high level, then let's talk about the integrations within AWS for CUP. So CUP integrates with the API Gateway and the Application Load Balancer natively, so for the API Gateway, we've seen how that works already, our users will authenticate with our Cognito User Pool, and retrieve the JSON Web Token from it, then they will pass the web token, the JSON Web Token, to the API Gateway, which will evaluate the Cognito Token and make sure that it is valid, and then, allowing us to access our backend, and this is how we provide authentication onto our API Gateway.

But, very simply, we can also use an Application Load Balancer, so using Application Load Balancer Listeners and Rules, we are able to authenticate our users against Cognito User Pools, and then once done, we can forward our users to the backend in our Target Group, which could be EC2 instances, Lambda functions, or ECS containers. So that's it for high level of Cognito User Pools, now let's do a hands on in the next lecture, to practice and see how they work in details.

lectures.title: Cognito User Pools - Others
lectures.text:
So, just a short theory lecture to reiterate on what I've said in the hands-on. So first, we can use Lambda Triggers so that the Cognito User Pools can invoke any Lambda function synchronously on some of these triggers, and we've seen most of them, but so, the important ones are going to be around the authentication events, so pre-authentication, post-authentication and pre-token generation, we can have a Lambda trigger, for example, to accept or deny your sign-in request, to log events after a successful authentication for custom analytics or to augment and suppress token claims.

Then for the sign-up, we can do a pre sign-up, post confirmation and migrate user Lambda trigger. This will be helpful, for example, in this one, to give a custom welcome message or event logging for custom analytics after a user has signed up. Finally, we can customize the messages that we send to the user thanks to a Lambda function, and finally, we can modify the token creation by adding or removing attributes in ID tokens. Another very nice thing about the Cognito User Pools is that we had a hosted authentication UI and that was allowing us not to program that UI in our application, we can just reuse the one Cognito has created for us, and with it we can handle the sign-up and signin workflows.

In using this hosted UI, we have a foundation with all the integration for social logins, OIDC or SAML, so we don't have to reprogram everything, and if we wanted to include this UI into our own application, then we can customize the logo, as we've seen, and we can customize the CSS to make it look like it belongs to our websites. So this will be a login screen with your own custom logo in big. Now for the hosted UI, you may want to host it on your own domain and therefore a custom domain.

So the trick you need to know is that if you're using custom domains with Cognito User Pools, regardless of where it is created, you must create an certificate for using HTTPS. That certificate must be in ACM, okay? And the region it needs to be in must be us-east-1. You have no other option. So, this is a trick because, well, even if you have a Cognito User Pool in, say eu-west-1, you must create it in us-east-1, your certificates. Now the custom domain, you must define it in the app integration section of Cognito User Pools because this is going to be a configuration for all app claims.

This is a general configuration. Another very nice feature of Cognito User Pools is adaptive authentication. So the idea is that you allow your users to sign-in as normal using their username and password, but then with adaptive authentication, in case there is a suspicious login, then the sign-in can be blocked or we can reqUIre multi-factor authentication. How does it work? Well, each sign-in attempt is going to be examined by Cognito, and then is going to be a risk score, low, medium or high for how likely the sign-in request is going to be from a malicious attacker or an unknown login, and so, if that's the case, then users may be prompted for a second multifactor authentication only when there is risks.

So you as a normal user, that Cognito is used to, maybe you log in from your own computer in your workplace, so you're good, you can sign-in using a password, but then if somehow you or someone else's tries to log in from a new location using your password again, Cognito may say, "Hm, that looks like a suspicious login. Please use MFA to verify your identity." So the risk score is based on many different factors, such as if the user is using the same device as usual, the location, the IP address, and so on.

And in case of compromised credentials, there is account takeover protection and there will be phone and email verification as well. On top of it, any kind of work done by the adaptive authentication mechanism is going to be seen in CloudWatch logs, such as the sign-in attempts, the risk score, the fail challenges, and so on. Now, when you log in with a Cognito User Pool, what you get back from the pool is a JWT Token or a JSON Web Token. And so these are Base64 encoded.

You'll have what's called the header, the payload and the signature, and so Base64 is allowing you to transmit that over the network easily, and then it's going to be decoded and it looks like this. So this is a JWT Token payload. The header is not represented, that's the first line and the token signature is not represented, that's the last line. What I've shown you is the payload, and the payload indicates a lot of information about the user. We'll go over it in a second, but first, when you receive a JWT, to trust what's in the payload, you need to verify the signature.

So, the signature is the thing at the very bottom, and there is an algorithm that allows you to say, "Okay, if the signature is correct then I can trust whatever information is in the payload, because otherwise, if that wasn't the case, you could declare here whatever user, and so there are libraries to verify a JWT Token, and once it's done, you can use the payload, and so the payload contains user information. So here for example, we have the sub UUID, which represents the user ID in the Cognito User Pool database.

So using that sub UUID, you could, for example, recover any kind of information you want about your user that you've stored in the Cognito database. So, from the Cognito database, you could recover, for example, the user email, the given name, the phone number, any attributes you've defined as part of your Cognito User Pool. Then there's some other fields we can look at. For example, you'll have the username, the Cognito groups. You may have also the expiry of this Jason Web Token, all of this, as part of the payload, but again, if you need extra information, please look up the user in the Cognito user portal database using the user ID with the sub UUID.

Okay, so that's it. We've seen all we need to know about Cognito User Pools. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Application Load Balancer - User Authentication
lectures.text:
So we know we can integrate Cognito with the API gateway to authenticate users, but we can actually do the very same thing with an application load balancer. So your ALB can securely authenticate user and this allows you to remove the work away from your application and have this responsibility put on your load balancer so that your applications can only focus on their business logic. So you can authenticate in multiple ways for your application load balancer.

The first one is to use an identity provider that is OpenID Connect, so OIDC-compliant. The second option is to use Cognito user pools and this is for social identity providers such as Amazon login, Facebook login, or Google login or if you have corporate identities that are compatible with SAML, LDAP, or Microsoft AD. So the first one, first option is to integrate directly without Cognito user pools and the second option is to use Cognito user pools, and I will show you them both in this lecture.

Now to make it work, you must set up an HTTPS listener, S for secure, and then you can set either the authenticate-oidc or the authenticate-cognito rules. So when you go and you configure your load balancer, you will see something like this where as you can see for this listener detail on HTTPS, the first default action is to authenticate and then to forward to your backend. Now in case your user is unauthenticated, what do we do? We have the option, we have three options.

The first one is to naturally say please authenticate. That's the default one. But you can also just deny the request altogether or allow the request altogether, and allow would be very helpful, for example, for your login page because people would access your login page without first being authenticated. So how does that work? Well, let's say we have an application load balancer connected to Amazon ECS and we want to implement a login through Amazon Cognito in which case the users will do GET/api/data.

Then the ALB is going to be set up with HTTPS with the action authenticate-cognito. So Cognito will do its thing and authenticate the user, and then the payload and the request is passed on to Amazon ECS with the added information of the user that was doing the request from Cognito. And this is very helpful because now you have more information to deal with with Amazon with your application, for example, with Amazon ECS, and you can return a specific response that is based on what the user information is.

So to set it up, it's very easy. You go to the ALB UI and then you would first create a Cognito user pool, a client, and a domain. You make sure that the ID token, the JWT token, is returned, but this is the default in Cognito user pools. Then you connect your Cognito user pool to your social or your corporate IdP if that's what you want, and then you set up several URL redirections and then you go ahead and you set up more callback URLs which are very specific to Cognito user pool so I don't wanna linger on this.

And then you just link that Cognito user pool into your ALB with the specific app clients and you're good to go. So it's quite easy. In case you're using OIDC authentication, there is a little bit more work because it's not using the Cognito integration. You can just integrate with any OIDC-compliant identity provider. So let's take the same example. They will be an HTTP requests. lectures.title: Cognito Identity Pools
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about a service that I wish wasn't named like this, but is named like this. It's the Cognito identity pools, also called Federated Identities. And I wish it wasn't named like this because it's so not the same as the Cognito user pool, but it's under the same umbrella of Cognito, which I don't like, but it's just my personal opinion. Let's try to understand what Cognito identity pools are. So our users are outside of our AWS environments, and they can be a web application users or mobile users, and they want access to stuff within our AWS environments.

So for example, they want to have access to DynamoDB table or an S3 bucket. And so to access these things, they need temporary AWS credentials. So we cannot create normal IAM users for these users because there are too many of them, it doesn't scale and we don't trust them. So instead, we are going to give these users access to AWS through a Cognito identity pool. So this identity pool can allow your users to log in through a trusted third-party.

And that could be a public provider, for example, log in with Amazon, Facebook, Google and Apple. Or even allow the users that are already logged in with the Amazon Cognito user pool or even allow OpenID Connect providers and SAML providers. Or, finally, the developer authenticated identities, which is a custom login server. So on top of all these login providers to allow to give our users their identity before they trade it for AWS credentials, we can allow unauthenticated guest users access into AWS.

So it is possible for us to define a guest policy and give our guest users AWS credentials. So once the users have obtained these AWS credentials, then they can access the AWS services directly with the API call using an SDK or through the API gateway. So these these credentials that the users get, they have an IAM policy that is defined by what we do in Cognito identity pools, and they can be customized based on the value of the user ID for fine grained control and we'll see this in this theory lecture.

So, I'll try to make it as simple as possible. So we have a web and mobile applications and they want to access our private S3 bucket and a DynamoDB table, but we want to make sure the users first get credentials of AWS, but we don't want to create an IAM user for these applications. So what do we do? We're going to leverage Cognito identity pools, but first we want the users to get a login and obtain a token out of this login. So we will allow our users to connect, for example, to a Cognito user pool, or to connect to Google login, Facebook login, so for social identity providers or SAML or Open ID Connect.

So they will log in with any of those. They will get a token and they will go and talk to the Cognito identity pool service to exchange the token for temporary AWS credentials. So first, the identity pool will verify the login with whatever provider we have defined. And then once it's validated, Cognito identity pool will talk to the STS service to get temporary credentials for our web and mobile application users. Once this is done, the credentials are returned to our applications and they can use and directly access AWS thanks to these credentials and the associated IAM policy.

So this is very simple and a big difference from what Cognito user pools are, but you see there's a lot of common, especially around the identity provider. So the question is how does it work if I use Cognito identity pools with Cognito user pools? So here's the answer. We have the same diagram. We want our users to connect to a private S3 bucket or DynamoDB table, but we want their identity to be stored in Cognito user pools. Okay, so this is the same diagram as before, but I'm just expanding into Cognito user pools.

So they're going to log in and get a token. And why would you do this? Well, maybe because we want all our users to be centralized in the Cognito user pools database. So it could be an internal database of users, or we can also enable social identity providers SAML and OpenID Connect as federated identity providers for our Cognito user pools. But nonetheless, all users are going to show up in my Cognito user pool. Then our web and mobile application users can exchange those JSON web tokens obtained from Cognito user pools into the Cognito identity pool for credentials so there will be verification of these tokens and then talking to the STS service to get these credentials that will be returned to our web and mobile applications.

And then thanks to these credentials, we will have direct access into AWS. If you understood this, I'm so happy and you're good to go for the exam. So how does Cognito identity pools decide which role to apply to which user? Well, we can define a default IAM role for both authenticated users and guest users. So that means the guest users will have one IAM role and the other will have another one's IAM role. And we can define rules to choose which role goes to which user based on the user ID.

And then we can customize the IAM policy thanks to using policy variables. And this will be allowing us to make sure that the users will only get access to what they need in DynamoDB or Amazon S3, for example. These IAM credentials are obtained by Cognito identity pools through the STS service with the API call named AssumeRoleForWebIdentity. And for it to work, the roles must have a trust policy of Cognito identity pools. So I'll make it a bit more concrete.

Here is an example. So we want to give our guest users access to AWS, and so we want to create an IAM policy, for example, that would allow any guest user to do a GetObject on a bucket for my_picture.jpg. So this would give us for the guest users access to AWS with a very simple, and obviously restricted, IAM policy. Then for the authenticated users, we can define a policy variable on Amazon S3. So our users are connected, but we want to make sure that they only have access to a prefix in your S3 bucket that represents what the user identity is.

And so as such, you can use a policy variable like here in green, and this is allowing a user to only access within the bucket we've defined, anything that starts with the prefix of its user ID. So effectively we gave the user access only to what it can access thanks to its user ID. And we can define the same on DynamoDB. So here is a sample policy in which we allow the user to do anything it wants on DynamoDB for my table, as long as the leading key for DynamoDB is corresponding to the user ID of the user.

So effectively we've done row-based security thanks to this IAM policy. Now these are advanced, but I just wanted to give you a sneak peek into how they worked. So that's it for this theory lecture. In the next lecture, we're going to practice Cognito identity pools.

And so because we have created an Amazon Cognito user pool before, we can just safely choose this one. If we want to also have guest access, so that anyone can access our pool and get IAM credentials out of it, we can enable guest access. So let's click on next, we have enabled both. Next, we need to configure permissions and so we need to create an authenticated role. This is a role that is going to be assumed by the users who are authenticating into our identity pool.

So I will call this one Cognito Identity Pool Authenticated Role Demo. And this role should contain the permissions that the user will have once they obtain access to AWS. So this is just minimal policy right now and we'll see how to add on roles after that, add on permissions after this. Next, for the guest role, again, we specify an IAM role, so this one is unauthenticated role demo and again, minimal permissions. So click on next. Next, because we have specified Amazon Cognito user pool as a source for login, we need to specify a pool ID as well as an app client ID, which we have created from before.

Now for the role settings, do we want to use the default authenticator role we have created for this specific pool or do you wanna have a role with rules? Now to get started, we need to set up an SDK and then integrate this into our code and then we authenticate a user thanks to the SDK and then we get the AWS credentials out of it. lectures.title: Cognito User Pools vs Cognito Identity Pools
lectures.text:
So, let's try to really understand the difference between Cognito User Pools and Identity Pool. But by now, you should have a good idea. So, Cognito User Pools is used for authentication which is identity verification. So it's going to be a database of users for your web and your mobile applications. And then you have federation for logins, so you can have social logins such as Google, Facebook, Amazon, or OIDC, or corporate logins using SAML. But the idea is that Cognito User Pools will be your database of users.

You can even customize the hosted UI for authentication, include your logo, and you have integration with Lambda during the authentication flow for pre-, for post, and so on. You can also adapt the sign-in experience to different risk levels, for example, with adaptive authentication. So that MFA is used in due time. Now for Cognito Identity Pools, this is for authorization or access control. And this is access control from within AWS. So, for just the comparison, if you have a mobile application and you just wanna have a database of users, you're good to go with Cognito User Pools.

But if you want these users to be able to access your AWS environment, for example a DynamoDB database or an S3 bucket, then you need to give them authorization, and this is achieved by using Cognito Identity Pools. So, here you will obtain temporary credentials for users and then the login to get these credentials, the way to exchange a token for these credentials can be done, again, by social, OIDC, SAML, which can be confusing but also Cognito User Pools.

And so, the idea is that wherever your user is identified then they can exchange this token for authorization. So you can use Cognito Identity Pool with Cognito User Pool, but you can also use Cognito Identity Pool on its own. The benefits also of using Cognito Identity Pools is that the users can be unauthenticated, they can be guests. And then, once you have them set up in Identity Pool, the users are going to be mapped to specific IAM roles and policies, and you can leverage policy variables, which gives them access to, for example, a DynamoDB table or an S3 Buckets.

So when you use Cognito User Pools with Cognito Identity Pools, you get authentication on the first hand and authorization on the second hand. And this is what I'm trying to represent in this diagram. So, let's say you have a web and mobile application, and you want to access your private S3 Bucket and DynamoDB Table with a per user type of security. So first, we'll do best practices. We'll do a login and get token from Cognito User Pools. So you'll have your internal database of users and you can federate the login using SAML, OpenID Connect, Google, or Facebook.

Then the user will have its identity will be verified. What we can do is that we can exchange then this token of your users for temporary AWS credentials. And the way it works out we can integrate Cognito Identity Pool directly with Cognito User Pools. Then we're going to get temporary credentials thanks to STS. And then the web and mobile applications can then issue API calls directly into AWS and we'll have made sure from Cognito Identity Pool that the IAM policy attached to these temporary credentials allow them to perform exactly the action they need.

Okay, so by now you should really be able to understand the differences between user pools and identity pools. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Step Functions Overview
lectures.text:
Now let's discuss AWS step functions. So step functions allow you to model a workflow as state machines and you have one state machine per workflow. So this could be used if you want to have an order fulfillment or data processing, a web application or any workflow you want. The idea is that you will define what happens and what happens next, and then what happens based on some condition and so on to define a workflow. So as you can see on the right hand side, there's a visual workflow.

We start and we have an example, is it yes or no? If it's no, then you go to the end. If it's yes, then you wait three seconds. Then you say, "Hello" and "World," you compile the result into "Hello World" and you go into end. So we'll be going through hands-on to make it specific but the idea is that you define a workflow in JSON and this JSON allows you to get a visualization of the workflow and then it gets executed visually, and then we can see the history of the execution itself.

So the idea is that every little step in the workflow is going to be, for example, a Lambda function or inserting data into DynamoDB or a specific ECS task, and the step function is going to be the thing that orchestrates this workflow for you. To start a workflow, you can use an SDK API call, you can use API gateway, you can use CloudWatch Events or Amazon EventBridge, they're the same thing, or you can launch, obviously, a step function manually from the console, as we will be doing it in the hands-on.

So step functions have a bunch of boxes as you see on the right hand side and these boxes are called tasks. And so the task state is used to do some work in your state machine. So the task state could be invoking a Lambda function or it could be invoking a Batch job or running an ECS task and wait for it to complete or to insert an item directly from step functions into the DynamoDB or to publish a message into SNS or SQS or even to launch another step function workflow.

All these things can be defined in a task state, or a task could also be running one activity and that activity could be an EC2 machine or an Amazon ECS task or on-premises server that is going to be pulling for some work from step functions to do the work and then send back the results to the step function. The idea is that here, we are more free in terms of that, the app server is not invoked by the step function, the step function at the app server is actually pulling for step functions to find activities and work to do.

Which is more similar to how a service called SWF worked in AWS. So I wanna make this super concrete. So let's say we want to define a task state to invoke a Lambda function. So we're going to define a JSON and as you can see, the name is "Invoke Lambda function," the type is task and the resource is Lambda function invoke. Then the parameters is the function name, so we specify the function name, and we pass it on input payload to our Lambda function.

Then we say next, to go to the next state, and the time out, to see if our Lambda function is timing out. So what can be states in step functions? We could have this Choice State, to test for a condition to send it to a branch or the default branch. It could be a Fail or Succeed State, to stop executing the step function workflow with a success or a failure. It could be a Pass State, simply to pass the input to the output or to inject some fixed data without performing some work.

It could be a Wait State, to provide a delay for a certain amount of time or until a specified date and time. It could be a Map State, to dynamically iterate steps, or a Parallel State to begin parallel branches of execution. What you need to remember from the exam perspective is most likely going to be the parallel states. So, and the task state that I showed you from before, obviously. So I wanna show you what happens visually. So we have a execution workflow and this is a workflow.

So we submit a job. We wait for X seconds. We get the job status. Is the job complete? Yes or no, if not wait again, and so there's a loop. And when the job is complete, either you get the final job status because you completed successfully or if the job failed, then you maybe go and deal with that failure, and all of this go to the end. So as the execution is started, we're going to start, submit a job. We're gonna wait for X seconds and the blue is whatever is in progress.

Then it goes into several loops and then the job status is done, and then we get the final job status and we go to the end, and this gives us a visual aspect of our step functions. So the step function is really is here to orchestrate whatever work you need to do, to define how your state machine is going to look like. What your workflow is going to look like, and I know that right now, this may be, what the hell is this talking about? This is very confusing.

I can do all of that in just one Lambda function to program, but I will show you in the next lecture, a hands-on on step functions. It should make a lot more sense, and then I will show you the whole power of state functions in the further lecture by talking about error handling. So I will see you in the next lecture for the hands-on.
