lectures.title: Step Functions - Error Handling
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about error handling in step functions and really define the whole power of step functions. So a step function will execute many small tasks and these tasks will do very little amount of work. For example, talk to an API and so on. But all the error handling should happen outside of these tasks by step functions themselves. And so when can we have errors for example? Well, if the state machine has a definition issue, for example, there is no matching rule in the choice states, or if a task fails, for example, a Lambda function throws an exception, we should not catch it in the Lambda function itself, we should catch it in the step function error handling mechanism.

Or a transient failure. For example, there's a network partition events. So we can have two types of error handling in step functions, a Retry to retry a task, or a Catch, to transition into a failure path. And you should do this in the state machine instead of the application code. Because you make the application way simpler and you have all very nice mechanisms as well as execution history of these retries and these catch directly in the step function history.

So we have predefined error codes. So States.All, too much any error name or State.Timeout, if the task ran longer than the timeout seconds or there's no heartbeat received from an activity. Or TaskFailed in case of an execution failure of the task itself. For example, as I said, an exception in a Lambda function. Or States.Permissions, because there is not enough permissions to execute some code. So the state itself also may report its own errors and you can catch them in the step functions.

So let's talk about the Retry for tasks or parallel states. So the Retry allows you to define what happens and how many times to retry based on some errors. So this gets evaluated from top to bottom. And so we have here in this example a Lambda function being run, and we have one, two and three retry that are happening. So the ErrorEquals match a specific kind of error. So here ErrorEquals Customerror, in case the Lambda function throws a customer error, or ErrorEquals TaskFailed, in case the Lambda function just fails but without throwing the custom error, or All to try to catch all kinds of errors that can happen within that Lambda function.

So interval seconds say, how long to wait before retrying? So in this example, one, so wait one second and retry it or this one 30 seconds, so wait 30 seconds and then retry it or this one, five seconds. Then we have the BackoffRate, which is how many times you want to multiply the delay after retry. So to implement exponential backoff, so two, two, and two, in this example, they're all the same. Then we have MaxAttempts, so how many times we should retry.

So by default, it's three and zero, if you should never retry it, but in this example, we have MaxAttempts two, MaxAttempts two and MaxAttempts five. And then whenever all the attempts are fulfilled and reach, then the Catch block will kick in. So in this example, as you can see, if you were to define all the Retry logic from within the Lambda function, we would make the Lambda function run for a very, very long time, obviously, and maybe would timeout.

But also if you wanted to change your error handling logic you would have to redeploy Lambda function. But in this example, we are defining the retries from outside the Lambda function, into our step functions. And so therefore, we could change the Retry and the error handling logic directly from within our JSON documents and we have a lot more flexibility. And the Lambda function itself executes with a small amount of time and very quickly. So next, if we exhaust all the retries then we go into a Catch.

And the Catch has a similar logic , it's evaluated to top to bottom and you have ErrorEquals and Next, so let's have a look. So in this example, we have this Lambda function and we're saying, okay, in case you find the ErrorEquals CustomError, then Next go to this state called CustomERrorFallback, which corresponds to the block right here. So we're saying, "Hey, if you encounter a custom error, please now go into the states," and the state is pass and maybe there is an exception and the end is true.

So really the idea is here you can say retry, retry, retry, and in case of too many retries, then catch this error and go into the next state and do something about it. And the ResultPath is a path that determines what input is sent to the state specified in the next field. And we'll have a deep dive on it in the very next slide. So the idea here really is to say, in case there are too many execution failures or some specific kind of errors, then we want to catch them and move on with our state machine.

And again, if this is something we define within our code our code may become very, very complicated. But if this is something that we define within our step functions, we have a lot of flexibilities into how we want to handle these errors. So let's do an analysis of how this ResultPath works because it is important to understand that going into the exam. So let's say we have this task and there's one catch, and the catch is saying, go to the next task for any kind of errors and the ResultPath, $.error.

So the $.error allows you to include the error in the inputs. So let's say for example that we have this input being foo bar, thanks to the ResultPath with define, which is $.error, the output is going to contain the foo bar as before, but also an error block which contains the error message itself and some information about the error. That means that when this output is passed on to the next task into the next state, we can, for example, analyze send some emails and so on and debug based on it.

So the ResultPath is how you pass the errors from the inputs into the output, into the next task. And this is something the exam can ask you on. So that's it for step functions. I hope you liked it. And again, let's go into a hands-on to really understand how to retries and catches work in step functions. So I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Step Functions - Wait For Task Token
lectures.text:
So let's talk about a step function feature called wait for task token. So the idea is that you have your step functions and you have your execution workflow but then you want to wait for a task token to be returned because you're waiting for something external. So you may be waiting for another AWS service to do its thing or human approval or a third-party integration or to call legacy systems. And so to do so, you're going to, in your task in step functions, append the .waitForTaskToken to the resource field.

And this is going to tell step functions to wait for a specific task token to be returned before the execution can move on. So for example, here we have a resource named sqs:sendMessage and then we waitForTaskToken. I will show you in the very next slide how that works. So the task is going to be paused until it's going to receive a task token back with either a SendTaskSuccess if everything works or a SendTaskFailure API call. So let's take an example of a workflow.

We start, we're going to check the client credits and this actually relies on an external service. So what do we do? We are going to call SQS with a task token. So we'll use the waitForTaskToken in the resource and then we pass in the input, of course, to the SQS queue in the message. But also, we're going to pass the task token so that the receiving application knows how to call back then step functions. So then your SQS queues may be pulled by whatever application you may have.

It could be Lambda functions, it could be ECS, it could be EC2, it could be a third-party server. It could be whatever you want, right? But you're going to process the message. And then, of course, you're going to get the message input body but also, you're going to get the task token. And then if it's successful or a failure, you're going to use a SendTaskSuccess API call in which you're going to pass the outputs of the processing but also the task token that was passed initially to your SQS queue.

And then once the step function workflow receives that API call with the correct task token and the correct output, then you can go on and, for example, do the rest of your workflow. But the benefit of this is that we were able to rely upon an external system to perform some processing before we got back into our step functions workflow. And this is how you can integrate with any kind of external mechanism. So that's it for this lecture I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Step Functions - Activity Tasks
lectures.text:
Now let's look at Activity Tasks in step function. So here we have what's called activity workers and they want to perform tasks from your step functions. lectures.title: Step Functions - Standard vs Express
lectures.text:
So we have different ways of running our step function workflows. The first one is to use a standard workflow. This is the default. The second one is to use express workflows. And within express workflows, we have the asynchronous workflows and we have the synchronous express workflows. So, we'll have a look at all of them. So, for the standard default step function workflows, the max duration of a single workflow is up to one year. The execution model is exactly-once execution and you may execute about 2,000 standard workflows per second, which is a good rate.

And in terms of execution history, you get up to 90 days in the console history or you can use CloudWatch to have more logs and you can keep the logs forever with log retention settings in CloudWatch. The pricing is going to be by the number of state transitions, so going from one state to another. And the use cases for using standard workflows is for non-idempotent actions such as, for example, payments processing. Next, we have the express workflows and as the name indicates, they're for short ones, so, up to five minutes of execution.

But you have extremely high capacity for extremely high rates. So, you have over 100,000 executions per second that you can do. So quite a bit of volume. Now, there is no way to track things in the console. The only way to get execution results and analysis is by using CloudWatch logs. And you're going to be billed by the number of the execution, the duration of an execution, and the memory consumption. So the use cases for express for Cloud would be, for example, to do IOT data ingestion, or streaming data, or mobile app backends and so on.

Now, within express we have asynchronous and synchronous and the main difference I want you to remember is that the asynchronous express workflow has at least once execution model guarantee, and the synchronous type of express workflow has at most once, and the exam will test you on this. So, when you're using an asynchronous express workflow the workflow, the execution just starts and we don't wait for the results and how do we know if it has ended, and if the result is correct, well, we'll have to check CloudWatch logs.

So, this is when you don't need an immediate response. For example, for messaging services, you just want to send a message, you just do it, but you don't wait for the response whether or not the message gets sent successfully. So because we have an at least once execution guarantee in case there are errors we can try again directly, automatically from within step functions and so it's possible for the same action to be done twice. And so in that case, you must manage at the idempotence to make sure that if you run the same action twice, you don't have twice the same effects.

For a synchronous, at most once, this is when we invoke an express workflow, but we wait for the workflow to complete and when we get the result out of it. So this is, for example, when you need an immediate response from the workflow itself. So, for example, if you orchestrate microservices and you want to make sure that everything is working correctly before you stop the execution. In that case, for synchronous workflows, you can invoke them from the API gateway or Lambda function and get a response from it.

And it's at most once because if there's a failure, the step functions will not restart the workflow for you. It's up to you to try again if you wanted to but that's the kind of logic that you need to implement. Okay, so that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: AppSync Overview
lectures.text:
Now let's talk about AWS AppSync and AppSync from an exam perspective, there's two angles to it. The first one is that it's a managed service that we uses GraphQL. So if she wants to build a GraphQL API on AWS, look no further than AppSync. What does GraphQL? Well, GraphQL makes it easy for applications to get exactly the data they need it's a new style of API. The idea is that you just ask for the fields you want and GraphQL returns just that's.

The idea with GraphQL though is that you can combine data from one or more sources into a graph, so that means that the data sets behind GraphQL, can include NoSQL data stores, Relational databases, HTTP APIs, and they're all combined together. GraphQL in AppSync has direct integrations with DynamoDB, Aurora, OpenSearch and other sources and you can get any data from anywhere if you want to with Lambda to extend the pattern. The second angle for using AppSync in AWS, is to have real time WebSockets integration or MQTT on WebSockets.

The idea is that if you're building a real time application that needs to access a data feel, you have many ways, but one of these ways is AppSync with a WebSockets. You could also use an application on the balancer or the API gateway, but AppSync is one of these options. Then if you have a mobile application and you want you to have local data access and data synchronization, AppSync is also a replacement for something we've seen that was outdated called cookie to sync.

So this can come up in the exam as well. Finally, to get started with AppSync, you just need to upload one GraphQL schema and We'll see this in the hands on. So, in a diagram we have AppSync in the middle, and to get start with AppSync, you need to create a GraphSQL schema. So we upload the schema and this is what a schema may look like. And then you have a client and the client will say, "Hey, I want you to do this query on AppSync?" And you're specifying, for example, in this research, the name of the human and then the fact you want its name, the fact that we want to know which movies it appears in and the Starships.

And then AppSync will run its own resolver, so this is the way, this is the magic of GraphQL. It works with resolvers and one of these results resolver may be DynamoDB so that means fetch the data from DynamoDB. And then AppSync knows how to automatically return the data in JSON form to the clients to comply exactly with the exact query that was asked. And as we can see, it is a very JSON. But with GraphQL you can ask for any fields and it will be returned automatically by AppSync.

So that's the general idea, obviously going into an exam, you do not know how to write a Schema or a query and so on. Just need you to know the high level, but I want to show you the behind the scenes. So at a high level AppSync has integrations for your web applications, your mobile apps that all use GraphQL, but also anything that's going to be Real-time. So it could be a Real-time dashboard, for example, or any application that needs offline data synchronization and a replacement for convene to sync.

For AppSync at its core you have GraphQL schema, you upload and resolvers to tell how to fetch data. For these resolvers we have direct integration with DynamoDB, Aurora, OpenSearch or anything you want through a Lambda function or an already existing public HTTP endpoints with the HTTP integration. And if you're an into log, anything that was happening in AppSync, it is integrated with CloudWatch Metrics and CloudWatch logs to get this information.

Finally, because we're creating an API in AWS, we need to talk about security. So there's four ways you can authorize applications to interact with your AppSync GraphQL API. The first one is with API_KEY, so you generate these keys just like for the API gateway and give them to users. The second one is use AWS_IAM to allow IAM users roles or across account access to your absent API, which is also very similar to what we saw for the API gateway. Then we have OPENID_CONNECT if you wanted to have an integration with an OpenID Connect provider and a JSONWeb Token and finally AMAZON_COGNITO_USER_POOL to integrate with already existing User pools, you upgraded in Cognito and through Cognito User pools, then you can federate through other social login providers for example.

Finally, if you want you to get HTTPs security on AppSync with a custom domain, the recommended solution is used CloudFront in front of AppSync. So that's it for this theory lecture we gonnaa hands on to get some practice.

lectures.title: AppSync Hands On
lectures.text:
Okay, so let's go ahead and practice using AWS AppSync. So we're going to create an API and we have two options. The GraphQL APIs or Merged API, which is a combination of GraphQL APIs. So we'll choose the first option because it is by far the simplest and the one you should know about. Then we're going to design this from scratch but you could also import from DynamoDB or create a real-time API. So we'll design it from scratch and we'll name it My AppSync API.

This is fine. And then click on next. So this GraphQL type can be backed by DynamoDB table so that the schema is configured and the data is stored. So we will create a type backed by DynamoDB table right now and the model name is going to be Student. Next, we're going to create fields for our students. So the first field is going to be an ID. So the type is ID and required, yes, but we can have, for example, a student name. So it's a type string and maybe it's required.

And then we can have a type age, which is going to be an int, not necessarily required, and then certified is going to be a Boolean and not required. Okay, so this is how we model our information. And then we need to configure the model table, which is what is the name of the table going to be in DynamoDB? So I can name it StudentTable. We have to select a primary key, for example, ID, and we don't need any sort key right now. So click on next. And we have designed our first API.

So let's create it. So my API is now created, and if I look at the schema, this was automatically created from the schema I have provided for my DynamoDB table. So by the way, we can go into DynamoDB, and we can check whether or not this table got created. So I'm going to go into tables and yes, we can find our StudentTable right here. So let's go back here. So we have a bunch of schema that is created and this is GraphQL-specific knowledge, so you don't need to linger over this.

Then data sources. So this is my DynamoDB table that is linked to my GraphQL API. Functions, we don't need to know about it right now. And queries, this is where we can start using this API. So as we can see here, we have the option to run what's called the createStudent mutation or the listStudents mutation. So for example, if I run the listStudents mutation, which is a GraphQL query, right now we see that there is no results in our query. So first, I need to create the students.

So we'll run the createStudent mutation and this takes inputs and this input comes from right here. So the name is, for example, we have Mike, age: 25. Certified: true. So let's run this right now, createStudent. So this is done and I can do another one. For example, Alice who is going to be 30, and she's also certified. So let's run this again. And now if I run the listStudents API from my GraphQL, as you can see, I get the list back. So we have Alice and we have Mike available right here from this API.

And in DynamoDB, if I go into explore table items, as we can see, both my items get stored and returned in my DynamoDB table. But the cool thing about it is that now we have a full GraphQL-compatible API on top of our DynamoDB table. So we can expose it to our mobile clients or any websites that is using GraphQL and API mechanism, which is very, very handy. We have caching type of settings. So we can have full request caching, per-resolver caching or no caching.

We have settings that we can edit. So we get, for example, the GraphQL endpoint. We get the API ID, the real-time endpoints, a bunch of information. We have the authorization modes, so is it an API key? And we can create new API keys if you wanted to as you can see right now. Or is it using IAM or OpenID Connect or Lambda or Amazon Cognito User Pool if you wanted to connect the authorization to Cognito. So we'll leave it as API keys. Then do we want to have additional authorization providers, which you can have multiple ones.

As you can see right here, you can select multiple ones. So this is cool. And then finally, monitoring for our API. So how many errors, how many requests, and so on. As well as finally, if you wanted to connect to custom domain names to host this under your own domain name. So that's an overview of AppSync. You don't need to know about GraphQL in great details. As you can see, once you have GraphQL, you can integrate it with JavaScript for your websites or Android or iOS for your apps.

So this is really meant to create a API that works for both web and mobile. And that's all you need to know that there is a link between GraphQL and AppSync and that you can back AppSync by your DynamoDB tables. So to finish this hands-on, just go and find your APIs, take it, and then you can delete it. So just enter the name again, My AppSync API, and this is going to delete all the AppSync level stuff. And of course, you also need to delete in DynamoDB your table.

So you do action and then delete table. No need to have a backup and we delete it and we're done. So that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: AWS Amplify
lectures.text:
Talk about AWS Amplify. And Amplify is a service that in a gist allows you to create mobile and web applications, and it's made of different components. We have Amplify Studio, which allows you to visually build a full stack app both the front-end UI and the backend. We have the Amplify CLI to do the exact same thing but with the CLI. Then we have the Amplify Libraries to connect your app to existing AWS services, such as Cognito for login or S3 for storage and so on.

And then Amplify Hosting, which is to host your Amplify application on AWS and deliver it very, very fast. So it can be quite complicated but let's go step by step to understand these components. So AWS Amplify first is a set of tools to get started with mobile and web applications. And you should think of it as the elastic beanstalk for mobile and web applications. So we start with Amplify Studio or the CLI, and for the CLI we type amplify in it, and it initializes our Amplify application.

So Amplify gives us must have features such as data storage, authentication, storage of data of files overall, and machine learning. All of this powered by AWS services. So in the backend, Amplify is relying on DynamoDB, AWS AppSync for GraphQL APIs, Cognito, Amazon S3, and so on. And then Amplify also gives you front end libraries. They're ready to use for different frameworks such as React, View, JavaScript, iOS, Android, Flutter, and so on. And so AWS Amplify is going to be a one-stop shop to integrate all these things together.

It incorporates the best practices for reliability, security, and scalability. And then to deploy this application we can use the Amplify CLI or Amplify Studio. And the exam may ask you about some important features of Amplify. So here they are. The first one is that Amplify gives you authentication out of the box. For this, we do amplify add auth, and this is leveraging the Amazon Cognito. You get user registration, authentication, account recovery, and other operations.

It supports MFA, social signing, et cetera, et cetera. And you get pre-built components to build this in your front end and integrate with Cognito. And finally you get your fine grain authorization. The second feature is around the datastore. So you do amplify add api, and it's going to leverage Amazon App Sync for the API and Amazon DynamoDB for the data storage. And the idea is that with Data Store, you work with local data, and then you have automatic synchronization to the cloud without any complex code thanks to the Amplify framework.

It's powered by GraphQL and AppSync overall, and it gives you offline and realtime capabilities, and you can even model your data with the Amplify Studio. Finally, we get Amplify Hosting. And this is when you want to start deploying your application. So you do amplify add hosting, and it allows you to build and host modern web apps. You do CICD, such as build test and deploy. You do your pull request previews, you have your custom domains, you can have monitoring, you can set up redirects and custom headers and password protection. So it looks like, for example if you know competing services such as Netlify Reversal, Amplify Hosting is similar.

And so you're going to get your code somewhere. So for example, GitHub or Bitbucket, GitLab, even CodeCommit. Then your CICD is going to build the front end in whatever you have and then deploy it, for example to CloudFront. And same, you can have the CICD to build the backend optionally and deploy the backend into Amplify. Also for Amplify, you have the option of running testing. And you have two kind of testing, you have unit testing and end-to-end testing.

So you can run end-to-end testings in the test phase in Amplify. And the goal of doing end-to-end test is that you can catch regressions before pushing code to production. So you use the test step to run any test commands at build time and you define the test steps in your amplify.yml file. And then you can use the Cypress testing framework to generate your end-to-end test. The benefits of using the Cypress testing framework is that you're gonna get a UI report for your test, and you can define web clicks.

So Cypress can generate and simulate a web browser and you can just say, "Click here, do this, do that and do that," and then verify whether or not that works. And that's called end-to-end test because we deploy the application and we verify whether or not the application is working as expected from a usability standpoint. So just to summarize, you have build level tests, which is when you are running unit tests when you build your application, and this is to test whether or not your code is supposed to do what it's supposed to do.

Then you have an end-to-end test, which is when the app is deployed. You're going to run end-to-end tests, for example using the Cypress framework, to make sure that it behaves the way it's supposed to behave. And then finally you can deploy your application. Okay, so that's it for Amplify. I hope you liked it. And I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: AWS Amplify - Hands On
lectures.text:
So let's go ahead and practice using AWS Amplify. So you click on create a new app, and here for getting a startup project, you click on here to visit the docs and the documentation is going to show us how to basically get started very quickly. So there is a repository we need to clone onto our own GitHub. So you click here and it's going to make you sign in into GitHub. And then when you're good to go, click on create repository. Now that everything is cloned, you can go back into your app and as a provider you will click on GitHub, click on next, and it's going to make you authorize the AWS Amplify console to read your repository.

So you go ahead in there and then you choose what you want to give access to. And then in here you select your Amplify VT React template that you just cloned. You click on next and then you leave the build settings on and then you will create and use a new service role automatically. So we come next and then save and deploy. And what's going to happen is that the Amplify is going to bootstrap our account to install whatever it needs to, for example, CDK to build everything.

So if you go under CloudFormation, actually you should start seeing things. Let's go into CloudFormation. As you can see, the CDK toolkit is an updating progress. So, or it can be created for you, depends on what you have. And then the Amplify service is going to build our application. So now my app has been built and I can click on this domain and access my to-do app. So to-do is pass my exam and also practice with practice questions. So as you can see, this is working and I can add some information into my to-do app.

And this was fully hosted by Amplify. You can always look at your stacks in CloudFormation to see what happens. So here we have multiple Amplify stacks. We have this one, and then we have four nested stacks within that have been created. And it's always good for you to have a look at what is being created as part of the resources. So it's up to you, but this app is managed by the CDK. Okay, so let's have a look next into the Amplify UI. So let me refresh this page.

So now you click on your production branch and you have access to more information on the left hand side. So we can look at the deployments, we can look at data and user management. So let's have a look at Data Manager. So this is the data of your Amplify app. And you can see the two records I have inserted from my to-do list are already in here in my data manager. So behind the scenes, if you go into DynamoDB, then you will see a table on the left hand side, which is my to-do table.

And if you do explore item tables, you will see that the items are already here. So it's good. But you can manage everything from data manager and you are able to create a to-do if you wanted to directly from here, you can even click on one and edit it if you wanted to. So more capabilities from within this UI as well as downloading everything as a CSV. For user management this is where you would set up your users and so you could create them and then start having security on top of your Amplify app.

And so to do so, you will need to create an authentication branch to it, and then push the necessary code to set up authentication. But then everything would be managed from here. And this has, for example, deep integration with Amazon Cognito. You can look at storage. So again, this gives you information can against the kind of storage you can have. And you can click here to view the storage of the configurations you can have, for example, here to set it up, you can create a backend storage and the backend could be backed by whatever you need.

So it could be Amazon S3 or other things as well. And then you function. So the functions are Amplify functions, and they're backed up by AWS Lambda. But again, this is all very much abstracted from this Amplify console, which is good because then you just focus only on the code itself and you let (indistinct) take care of all the infrastructure. And then you have a UI library. So you can, for example, take some UI components or do Figma-to-React and so on directly from within the Amplify console.

So this is very handy. And of course if you were to do changes, then you would redeploy an application version and automatically thanks to CICD, the build would happen and the deploy would happen as well. So Amplify is just at a high level, very, very powerful. You can also explore if you wanted to, anything around custom domains, build notification, build settings, environment variables and so on. And this is something you would find in competing services such as, for example, Netlify or (indistinct).

But I like the fact that on Amplify everything is on your AWS account, so everything is private, which could be quite handy. So that's it, you don't need to know too much about Amplify, just the fact that you have an all in one shop to build and deploy your applications on AWS, which is very, very handy, again. So to just be done, you go to your app settings, and then under general settings you can delete the app, you type delete, and this is going to clean up any kind of resources that has been deployed.

And of course you could go on your GitHub and also delete your repository by just scrolling all the way down and doing delete. And yes, I want to delete the repo, and then you enter the repo name and you're good to go. Okay, so that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: STS Overview
lectures.text:
So let's talk about STS, which is a Security Token Service. So STS allows you to get temporary security credentials up to one hour to access those resources directly. And so there's a bunch of API you need to know them at a high level going into the exam. So the first one is AssumeRole, to assume roles within your accounts or cross accounts, which is fundamental. AssumeRoleWithSAML in case your users are logged in with SAML, this is allowing us to get them allowing them to get temporary credentials.

AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity to return roles for users if they're logged with an identity provider. So Facebook Login, Google Login, or OIDC compatible. But we don't use this really anymore. Now we use Cognito Identity Pools instead. Instead of AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. Then we have GetSessionToken and we will see this very in-depth so this is when you have MFA for a user or AWS root account. Then GetFederationToken to get temporary credentials for a federated user.

GetCallerIdentity, which is return details about the IAM user or role used into the API call. So if you don't know who you are while using AWS, just call the STS GetCallerIdentity and you'll get information about who you are and what's your account number. And then we've seen that one as well in the beginning. DecodeAuthorizationMessage to decode an error message when it AWS API is denied. So the most important ones going into the exam is going to be AssumeRole, GetSessionToken, GetCallerIdentity and DecodeAuthorizationMessage.

So STS can assume, can be used to assume a role, so let's see how that works. So first we define an IAM role in our accounts if we want to AssumeRole within our accounts. Or in another account if you want to do cross-accounts. Then you define which principles can access this IAM role and we authorize everything with IAM policies. And then we would use the STS API to do the AssumeRole API call to impersonate the IAM role we have access to. Then the credentials valid between 15 minutes up to one hour.

So in the diagram, our users wants to access a role within the same or another account. And to do so, it's going to do the AssumeRole API onto STS. STS will check the permissions are correct or not. And then will return to us the temporary security credentials, which would allow us to act as if we were the role. Then for cross accounts access, this is pretty similar, we would create the role in another account. Then we would write the correct permissions in to our own account and the target account, and finally run the AssumeRole API to access the target accounts.

And for example, the role allowed us to access an S3 bucket, then we can access that S3 bucket in to our account, great. Finally, for STS with MFA, so this is very important to understand, going in to certified developer exam. So for this, you use the GetSessionToken API from STS to get a session token. Once you're logged in with an API with an MFA device, and we've seen this in the CLS section. Then we need the IAM policy with the proper IAM conditions.

And then in the IAM policy, you need to add this aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent:true, which is very explicit and this looks like this. For example, this role only allows us to stop instances or terminate instances only if we have MFA on, so MultiFactorAuthPresent:true. And this is how we would use it. So GetSessionToken is the API to use, and why is it? Well because it returns an Access ID, a secret key but also a session token that we have to include.

So three things to do our API call, and the last one, GetSessionToken returns the expiry date of our credentials, so we know when to renew them. Okay, so that's it for STS, I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture!

lectures.title: Advanced IAM
lectures.text:
So going into the exam, we need to have a much better understanding of advanced IAM concepts. So this lecture is going to be dedicated to explaining to you a few things that you think are granted but it's always good to see them outlined in diagrams. So the first one is the authorization model and how policies are evaluated. So since this is a simplified model by the way, it's a lot more complicated, but hopefully that gives you a good idea about how that works.

If there's an explicit deny in your policy then you end the decision with a deny. If there's an allow, you end the decision with allow. And else, you deny. So what does it look like? Say for example, that a user wants to create a DynamoDB table, the decision starts with deny. So by default, it can't do it. Then all the policies attached to that user will be evaluated. So for example, if we have a policy attached to our user, this will be what goes into this all applicable policies.

Then we'll look at the policy. Is there an explicit deny in the policy? Is there somewhere in the policy that says, "Users cannot create DynamoDB tables"? If so, the final decision is deny, no matter what. Then, only then, the allow will be evaluated. So is there an allow statement, allowing the user to create a DynamoDB table? Yes, then the final decision is allow. No, then the final decision is deny. lectures.title: Granting a User Permissions to Pass a Role to an AWS Service
lectures.text:
So, here is another feature we've been using in IAM without really knowing it, but it is crucial to understanding AWS. So when we configured many AWS services, we gave them IAM roles and for this the keywords that we passed IAM roles to them. And this was done, usually, when we set up a service the first time. So then the service, once it has an IAM role, it can assume the role and perform the actions it needs. So when we pass a role to another service, well, for example, when we created an EC2 instance role and assigned it to the EC2 instance we actually passed that role.

Or to a Lambda function where we created an IAM role and then we passed it to learn the function so that it could, for example, call Amazon S3 or an ECS task or when we passed a role to CodePipeline, to allow it to invoke other services. So all in all, when we want to pass a role to another AWS service we need the IAM permission called iam:PassRole and often this comes with another permission called iam:GetRole to view the role being passed. So the key here, though, is that to pass a role to another service you need the IAM pass for all permission.

So concretely what does an IAM policy look like? Well, it looks like this. So this IAM policy, if it was assigned to me, allows me to do anything I want on EC2 such as creating instances, terminating them etc. etc., but the second part of the statement allows me to pass a role, and that role is called S3Access. So that means that the only role I can assign onto my EC2 instances is this one S3 access role. And so for this I need the action iam:PassRole to do it.

So the question is, can any role be passed to any service? And the answer is no. Roles can only be passed to the services based on what their trust allows, and so a trust policy for a role is an indication to say to which service can assume that role. So here is a normal IAM role, so this is a trust policy for an IAM role. And this is saying that only the EC2 service, so this is in the principal service EC2, only this EC2 service has the trust to allow to assume that role and so we've been using this without knowing in the IAM policy, so let's have a look.

But in IAM I go to roles and we can see here there's a role name and here there is a trusted entity, and so this allows a specific service to assume that role. So, for example, if we look at this AWS CodePipeline service and we open it we can see the permissions we have allowed on this CodePipeline service they're here in JSON, but the second time in here is called Trust relationships and this trust relationship is a policy document. So I'll click on Show policy document and this is the trust policy which allows the CodePipeline service to assume that role.

So this is why here you see that the trusted identity providers are codepipeline.amazonaws.com, so this is the whole idea behind trust policy. But, you can have a look, there is a list of all the trusted entities in here. So if I scroll down, for example, and look at my Lambda functions so if I go to Lambda and look at lamda-dynamodb-demo-role, so this has a bunch of policies, but if I go to the trust relationship we can see the trust providers is lambda.amazonaws.com, which is, if I look at the JSON document, something like this.

So that's it, this was the behind the scenes. So, again, to pass a role we first need to create the correct trust relationship, to allow the target service to assume it, and then finally we need to have the iam:PassRole permission to pass the role onto the target service. So that's it for me. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: AWS Directory Services
lectures.text:
Okay. So now let's talk about Microsoft active directory and AWS directory services. So in case you don't know what Microsoft AD is, it is a software that is found on any windows server with AD domain services. And it's a database of objects and you objects can be user accounts computers, printers, file, share security groups. So all your users manage within your entire Microsoft ecosystem on premise is going to be managed by Microsoft active directory.

And there's going to be a centralized security management. You can create account, assigned permissions and so on. And all the objects will be organized into a tree. And a group of tree is called a forest, that's just for some terminology. So, let's take an example. We have a domain controller and we're going to create an account on it. We create an account. Username is "John" and the password is "password". And the idea is that all the other windows machines we have within our network are going to be connected to the domain controller so that, if we're using the John password on the first machine, is going to look it up in the controller and say, yes, we have that login and then allow you to log in from that machine.

So all these machines are going to be connected to your domain controller, and that allows you to have the users accessible on any single machine. So that's the whole idea behind active directory in a very, very high level. Now we have AWS directory services, which is to provide you a way to create an active directory on AWS. And we have three flavors on it. We don't have to do a deep dive on them but you have to understand the differences between these three flavors.

The first one is AWS, manage Microsoft AD to create your own active directory in AWS. And you can manage users locally and it supports multifactor authentication. The idea is that with this standalone active directory you can also create a trust connection with your on premise AD, where you have your own users there as well. And what that means is that your AD in here, for example, can be trusted with the on premise AD. So AWS trust the on-premise AD and on-premise AD trust AWS.

And so that means that if your users authenticate it to the rights, use an account that is not managed by AWS, It can go and look up the accounts into the on-premise active directory. And, similarly, if an on-premise directory user goes and authenticate to your on premise AD using the a AWS accounts, it can be trusted to go and look it up. So here our users are going to be shared between our on-premise active directory and AWS. Okay. A little bit complicated.

I know if you're new to this, but hopefully it makes sense. The AD connector is a little bit different. This is a direct gateway proxy to redirect to on-premise AD and it supports MFA, if you need multifactor authentication And the users are solely managed into the on-premise AD. So here is the example. In this example, our AD connector is just acting as a proxy. So if the users to you authenticate with our AD connector, it's going to proxy the request back to our on-premise AD and look it up.

So the idea here is that, in the first case with Microsoft manage Microsoft AD, we have users sitting in AWS manage AD and users sitting in on-premise AD. Whereas, with AD connector, as the name indicates, it connects the proxies, the queries, the, the connection request back to our on-premise active directory and the only place where we can manage users is going to be on the on-premise AD. Finally, you have simple AD and it's an AD compatible managed directory on AWS.

It doesn't use Microsoft directory. And it cannot be joined with a non-premise active directory. So, the idea is that if you don't have an on-premise AD and you need an active directory for your AWS cloud, then you can have just a simple AD as a standalone thing. And the idea here is that, using active directory, you can create easy two instances that are going to be running windows. lectures.title: Encryption 101
lectures.text:
Okay, so in this lecture, if you're not too familiar with how encryption works, I want to give you a little bit of details on how it works at a high level. So, first let's talk about encryption in flight, which is going to be referred as TLS or SSL. TLS is the newest version of SSL. So what we have is that the data is going to be encrypted before sending the data. And then it will be decrypted after receiving it. So this is for communication between a client and a server over a network.

And so what's going to be happening is that for encrypting the data TLS certificates are going to be used. And this is what you see when you go onto websites and it says HTTPS, that means that the connection between you and the server is going to be encrypted using TLS certificates. Why do we want encryption in flight? Well, because we're sending data over a network and sometimes a public network and the data goes around many different servers. We don't want to be having a man in the middle attacks where a middle server receives the data and just observes the packages we're sending to the server.

And so what we want to have HTTPS or TLS, or SSL, this is when we know that only the target server can decrypt the encrypted data we're sending. So let's take an example. We have a client and a server and we want to be able to securely login into the server by providing our username and password. But we only want the target server to be able to receive it. So we're going to have the username and password and then we're going to apply TLS encryption on the client side automatically.

The data is going to be encrypted and sent over the network. So as you can see, no between server can decrypt the data and only the target server can use the TLS decryption mechanism to decrypt that package and then see that we've sent the username and password. And therefore say that we're securely logged in. So that's for encryption in flight. The next one is around the server side encryption at rest. The idea is that the data will be encrypted after being received by the server so that it's stored securely.

And then it will be decrypted before being sent back to our clients. It will be stored in an encrypted form thanks to a key, and that key is usually a data key. And so the whole idea of managing these keys for encryption and decryption is that the management must happen somewhere and the server must have access to these keys. So let's take a service, for example, Amazon S3. We're sending an object over HTTP, maybe even HTTPS for inflight encryption.

And so the service receives our object, but it is decrypted. So the service can use a data key, and using the data key and the decrypted objects, we can have encryption of that object at rest. And then when it comes to sending back that object to the clients, the encrypted objects and the data key will be used together to decrypt. We'll have a decrypted form of object, and then that object will be sent over HTTPS back to the clients. So we received the decrypted object as is.

As we can see in this case, there is a server side encryption because all the encryption and decryption happens on the server. So finally let's talk about client-side encryption. And the idea is that this time the data is encrypted and decrypted at the client side. And the server should never be able to decrypt the data because we don't trust a server in that case. So for this, we could leverage encryption for this mechanism. So let's have an example.

The client has an object and the data key this time is client side. And after encryption, we get an encrypted object. That encrypted object can be sent then securely to any storage service available, an FTP server, Amazon S3, EBS volumes, et cetera. And they will be stored in encrypted form. So the entire server can not even decrypt the data contents. When we retrieve the contents, we retrieve the encrypted object directly. And if we still have access to the data key client-site, then we're able to perform the decryption mechanism and get the decrypted objects back.

So that's it for the three encryption mechanisms we can see in the Cloud. I hope you liked it. And I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: KMS Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about AWS KMS, which is a key management service of AWS. So we've been using it a lot without knowing, but anytime you hear encryption when you have an AWS service, it's most likely going to be KMS encryption. The aim is that with this KMS service, AWS is going to manage the encryption keys for us. And that's great, because that means that we have less things to do. So KMS is, of course, fully integrated with IAM for authorization, and it gives us very easy ways to control access to our data if it's encrypted with KMS.

The power of using AWS KMS is that you're able to audit every single API call made to use your keys through CloudTrail, which is something the exam may test you on. So on top of it, KMS can be used seamlessly into most AWS services. So for example, if you wanted to encrypt the data at rest in an EBS volume, just enable the KMS integration. Same for S3, same for RDS, same for SSM, and same for pretty much all the services that require encryption.

The idea is that with KMS, you can also use it yourself. And if you have secrets data, you never ever store them in plain text, that means just as is. Especially in your code. So if you want to use KMS, you can also use KMS through API calls. You can use the AWS CLI or the SDK. And that means that you can encrypt whatever is a secret for you with a KMS key. And then these encrypted secrets can be, for example, stored in your code or in environment variables.

That is a much better pattern. So now let's talk about the different types of KMS keys available to you. So now it's called a KMS key. By the way, it used to be called the KMS customer master key, but it was confusing because there's also the customer managed keys as we'll see in a second. So now, we just talk about KMS keys. So we have two types of KMS keys. We have the symmetric KMS keys, and that means there's only one single encrypted key that is used to encrypt and decrypt data.

And so any service of AWS that is integrated with KMS will use symmetric keys. The idea is that when we create or use a KMS symmetric key, then we never get access to the key itself, okay? All we do is that we use the KMS API calls to leverage and use that key. The second kind of key available on KMS are called asymmetric keys. That means that you have two keys. You have a public key that's used to encrypt data, and a private key used to decrypt data.

So this is used when you have encrypt/decrypt, or sign/verify type of operations. And in that case, you can download the public key out of KMS, but you can use access the private key. You can only use API calls against to access the private key. So the use cases for an asymmetric type of key is when you want the encryption to be done outside of your AWS cloud by users who cannot or don't have access to the KMS API key. In which case they will use the public key to encrypt the data.

Send it over to you. And you within your account, you would use the private key of AWS to decrypt that data. So within the world of KMS keys, you have different types of KMS keys. The first one are AWS owned keys. They're free, and this is the kind of key you would use when you use SSE-S3 type of encryption, or SSC DynamoDB, where you have the option, for example, that you choose a key owned by DynamoDB. So these are not really KMS because you don't really see them, but they're types of encryption keys within AWS.

Then you have the AWS managed keys, and they're free, and you will recognize them because they start with AWS slash and then the service name. For example, AWS/RDS or AWS/EBS, or in this example, AWS/DynamoDB. They're free and you can just use them as you please, but only from within the service that it's assigned to. Then you have your own customer managed keys and their custom keys, and they cost you $1 per month. And if you want to import them as well, you can import them, and they cost you $1 per month.

KMS also has a pricing where you're going to pay for each API call made to the KMS service, which is about 3 cents per 10,000 API calls. You also have automatic key rotation. So if it's an AWS managed KMS key, then it's automatic every one year. And if it's a customer managed key, you can enable automatic rotation and you set the period, and you can also have on-demand rotation of your key. And if it's imported KMS key, then you can only manually rotate it.

And for this, you need to leverage an alias. So KMS keys are scoped per region. That means that if you have an EBS volume encrypted with KMS key in a region, for example, EUS2, then if you want to copy that to a different region, we have to do several steps. First of all, we have to take a snapshot of this EBS volume. And if we take a snapshot from an encrypted snapshot, then this snapshot itself will also be encrypted with the same KMS key. Then to copy the snapshot to another region, we need to re-encrypt the snapshot using a different KMS key.

And this is something AWS will do for you. But the same KMS key cannot live in two regions. So now we have an EBS snapshot, it's encrypted with KMS with a different key, and it lives in another region. Now, we restore the snapshot into its own EBS volume with KMS, and it's KMS key B into the region AP southeast two. Now, the other thing we need to know about is KMS key policies. So this is to control access to your KMS keys. It's similar to an S3 bucket policy.

With a difference that if you don't have the KMS key policy on your KMS key, then no one can access it. So in that regards, we have two types of KMS key policies. We have the default one, and it's created if you don't provide a specific custom KMS key policy. And the idea is that the default allows everyone in your account to access this key. That means that if you have an IAM policy allowing a user or role to access this key policy, you're good.

But if you want to have more specific controls over it, you could use a KMS key policy that is custom. In which you define the users, the roles that can access your KMS key. And you define who can administer the key. And this is especially helpful if you want to do cross account access for your KMS key, because we can authorize another account to use our KMS key. So when do we use this? Well, for example, if we wanted to copy an encrypted snapshots across accounts.

So we create a snapshot encrypted with our own KMS key, and it's a customer managed key. It must be that because we need to attach a custom key policy. And then we attach a KMS key policy to authorize for cross account access. It looks like this. Then we share the encrypted snapshot with the target account. And then in the target account, we create a copy of the snapshot and we encrypt it with a different customer managed key in that target account.

And then we can create a volume from the snapshot in the target account, and we're done. So that's a lot of information by KMS, but let's go into hands-on to hopefully learn a bit more about it.

lectures.title: KMS Encryption Patterns and Envelope Encryption
lectures.text:
So now let's do a deep dive into how KMS really works for the encrypt and decrypt APIs as well as for envelope encryption. So what we did is that we had a secret, for example, a password, and it was less than four kilobytes, because this is a limit for KMS, and we sent it into the KMS service. So we use the encrypt API using an SDK or the CLI, and then we specified the CMK we wanted to use in KMS. And then KMS was checking with IAM if we had the right permissions.

And if we did, then it would perform encryption for us. What KMS will send us back would be the entirely encrypted secret. So that will be the encrypted data. Then we need to decrypt it. So we use the CLI or the SDK to do a decrypt API. And then we would, KMS would automatically actually, understand which CMK was used for encryption and look at it for performing decryption. It would first check with IAM to make sure that we have the correct permissions to perform the decryption.

And if we do, then it would send us via decrypted secret in plain-text. So this is the encrypt and the decrypt API and these are pretty easy. So as we can see though there is a problem, we are limited by the size of the secret to four kilobytes. So for this we have a loop encryption. So if you want to encrypt over four kilobytes, then there's this technique where you encrypt using an envelope. And the main API you have to remember for us to encrypt a large number, large amount of data is to use the GenerateDataKey API.

So from an exam perspective, if you want it to just stop here in this lecture, anything over four kilobytes of data has to be encrypted using the envelope encryption technique, which corresponds to the KMS GeneratDataKey API. Now I want you to go over the exam. So I want to explain to you how this API works and I think this could be valuable, but rest assured this is a little bit difficult. So if you don't follow, don't worry too much. So we're going to go into envelope encryption.

So we have the KMS service, and this time we want to encrypt a very big file. Maybe it is up to 10 megabytes, but it could be as big as you want, really. So we're going to use the SDK, and call the GenerateDataKey API, and we'll specify a CMK, and so KMS will check again the IAM permission, making sure we can generate a data key. And if we can, then KMS will generate this data key for us, and will send us back a plain-text version of it. So we have a plain-text data key encryption, data ecryption key, which is DEK.

So now we have this data encryption key, but why do we have it? Well, because now we can do something client side. We can encrypt the big file client side using our own CPU with this DEK. So this gives us an encrypted file. And then, actually, we're going to build an envelope around it, which is the final file. So we will build an envelope and what do we put in this envelope? Then we'll put an encrypted version of the DEK, and actually KMS will also send us this.

So when we call the GenerateDataKey API, it sends us both the plain-text DEK and the encrypted DEK. And so we store these two things into one final file. And this is why it's called envelope encryption. Because there is a wrapper around your encrypted file with the encrypted DEK. So as we can see in this example, from KMS the only thing we got was an encryption key, a data key and a data key that was encrypted. And all the work for the encryption of that file happened client side.

So now how do we decrypt that envelope? So to do so we come back from this envelope file, which contains the encrypted DEK and the encrypted file. And we're going to leverage KMS obviously one more time. So this time we're going to call the decrypt API. So with a decrypt API we can only pass up to four kilobytes of data. So what we're going to decrypt in this instance is going to be the data encryption key, so the DEK. So I'll pass through KMS, we'll check the IAM permissions.

And if everything is good with KMS, we're able to decrypt that DEK. So now we get the plain-text DEK. And with this plain-text DEK, we can look at the encrypted file and the plain-text DEK and decrypt it together, client side. And here we go, we have a decrypted big file. So the whole purpose of this envelope encryption technique is to use KMS for what it's good at, which is to generate keys, and then the whole encryption and decryption happens client side.

So this is complicated to implement, and so as such, AWS has implemented envelope encryption for us. And for this we can leverage the AWS encryption SDK. So this also exists as a CLI tool that we can install. And there are SDK implementation for Java, Python, C and JavaScript. And so on top of implementing this encryption pattern that I just showed you, this encryption SDK has a feature called data key caching. So in this example, instead of recreating a new data key every time we want to encrypt an object, we can reuse them instead.

And so the idea with reusing data keys is that you have less calls into KMS. So you are doing less API calls and it's less expensive. But there is a security trade-off because now you're using the same data key encryption, data encryption key for many different files. So it's a trade-off between your security and your API calls. But in practice this is still used. So if you're using data key caching, then you would use something called a LocalCryptoMaterialsCache, which has a long name, to indicate how big the cache of this data key should be.

And it could be that you define the max age of your key, the max number of bytes that it should encrypt, or the max number of messages that should be encrypted by this DEK before moving on to the next DEK. So this encryption SDK is extremely helpful. Now from an exam perspective, what do we need to remember? We need to remember the name of the symmetric APIs. So the first one is encrypt, to encrypt up to four kilobytes of data through KMS. The second one is GenerateDataKey, and this will generate a unique symmetric data key or DEK, and this API will do two things, it will return to us a plain-text copy of the data key and it will return to us an encrypted version of the data key with the CMK that we specify.

And this is what we've used during the envelope encryption. There's another API called GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext and this time it's to generate again a GEK, but not to use right now, it's to use at some point in the future. And so as such, this DEK is the same, it's also encrypted using this CMK we specify, but if you use it, we must decrypted afterwards, which is one extra step. So the exam will try to trick you to perform envelope encryption right now, you need to use GenerateDataKey API not GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext.

And then to decrypt anything, you need to use the decrypt API. So to decrypt up to four kilobytes of data, including an envelope encryption to decrypt the data key, the data encryption key. And finally, if you want it to generate a random number, then you have the API called GenerateRandom that will return a random byte string. So that's it for this lecture. I hope that was helpful to you and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: KMS Limits
lectures.text:
So, KMS is an inner service and therefore there are some request quotas. But KMS is extremely important. So in case you will exceed a request quota of KMS for encryption or decryption, for example, you will get a ThrottlingException. That will look something like this. It will say, "Status Code: 400; Error Code: ThrottlingException;" you are exceeding the right at which you can call KMS. So to respond to such and exception, we already know this, we can use exponential backoff, which means you can backoff and retry with an exponential time in between each calls.

But KMS has something very specific to it. Each cryptographic operation, so all of them decrypt and crypt and so on, they all share a quota. That means that any service that makes request on our behalf, for example, AWS S3 that uses SSE-KMS data encryption. Every time AWS will use that key for us, then it will be part of that quota. So we share a quota across our account for each region across all cryptographic operations. So that means that if we use our key too much, then we will get a ThrottlingException.

So what can we do to solve it? Well, number one, if we're using the GenerateDataKey API then we can use DEK cachings. So cache the data encryption key locally so that we reduce the number of API calls done onto AWS and that is a feature of the encryption ID kit itself. The other thing we can do is to generate a request quota increase in case we are indeed going over that limit way too many times. And so, for this, we can request a quota increase through either an API call or by opening a ticket with the AWS support.

So what you want to remember here, is that there's two ways to go with that quota. So as I said, all these operations will share the same quota so should you decrypt, encrypt, GenerateDataKey, GenerateRandom, etc., etc. All these things are called cryptographic operations and they share the same quota. So depends on the region you're in to know what the quota value is. But so for the symmetric CMK quota you have 5,500 shared but in some regions you have up to 10,000, so shared across all this API called.

And in other regions you have 30,000 per second, again, across all these API calls. So if you somehow reach that limit, then you need to make a service limit increase to increase that shared quota for all the cryptographic operations. So that's it. So the three ways to deal with a KMS Throttling is number one, exponential backoff that is, if it's transient. Number two, to reduce the API calls into KMS is to use the envelope encryption SDK on top of the data encryption key caching feature.

And finally, number three, is to simply request a limit increase from AWS. So that's it. I will see you in the next lecture.

So now let's talk about a cool new settings for your S3 Buckets using it with SSE-KMS encryption. And this is a new setting which will allow you to decrease and wait for it. The number of API calls made to KMS from Amazon S3 when you use the SSE-KMS type of encryption by 99%. Which will reduce the cost of your overall KMS encryption used by Amazon S3 by also 99%. And how does this work? Well, this leverages data key and more importantly, this thing called an S3 bucket key.

So how does that work? Well, a customer master key and KMS is going to be used to generate a data key for your Amazon S3 Bucket once in a while and this key will rotates. But, once in a while and this key's called an Amazon S3 Bucket key. And this key is what's going to be used to encrypt objects in your Amazon S3 Buckets with KMS encryption. So this is a special one. And if you wanted to explicitly authorize a specific user, it could be whatever user, it could be a user, an IAM role, it could be a federated user, for example, as you can see in this example on the right-hand side.

You could, for example, allow which KMS actions you want, such as encrypt, decrypt, et cetera, et cetera. And then you explicitly outline the principle. In that case, the federated user in this example, does not need, additionally, an extra IAM policy to use your KMS key because it's been explicitly allowed in the KMS key policy. So what kind of principles can we explicitly allow in KMS key policies, but also in anything IAM? Well, we have the account and the root user.

So when you define something like this, such as principle AWS and the new account number, or the account number, and then route, you allow every principle within the accounts, okay? And then IAM policies kick in. Next, you can authorize a specific IAM role by outlining the role arn directly in the principle statements. You have IAM role sessions, so this is when you have an assumed role, or when you have an assumed identity through Federation. For example, for Cognito identity or SAML.

You also have AIM users when you outline a specific user in your accounts, or of course, in other accounts. You have federated user sessions. This is what we've seen before. So when you have user federation in AWS, you can specify a specific federated user, and then you can also allow a specific service. So you can see the principle now has a service to allow specific services to use your KMS key. Or if you wanted to allow everything and everyone, you can just use a Star or AWS star.

lectures.title: CloudHSM Overview
lectures.text:
So we have seen KMS for encryption, but now let's look at CloudHSM. So with KMS, AWS will manage the software for the encryption and will have control over the encryption keys. But with CloudHSM, AWS will provision some encryption hardware. It's called an HSM device, so a dedicated hardware, which is a hardware security module. And then we are going to manage our own encryption keys entirely, not AWS. So we have full control over the encryption keys.

The HSM device is going to be set up within the cloud of AWS, but it is tamper resistant with FIPS 140-2 Level 3 compliance, which means that if anyone tries to access your HSM device manually, then they're going to be stopped and blocked. The CloudHSM device supports both symmetric and asymmetric encryption keys. So that means that you can have, for example, SSL and TLS keys on top of it. There is no free tier and to use the CloudHSM device, you need to use the client software, which is quite complicated and out of scope right now.

There is an integration between Redshift and CloudHSM if you wanted to leverage CloudHSM for your database encryption and key managements. CloudHSM is a really, really good candidate if you want to implement SSE-C type of encryption on top of S3, for example, because you are managing your own encryption keys and you are storing them into this CloudHSM. So with the CloudHSM, AWS will manage your hardware, whereas the service itself can be used on your own.

The CloudHSM client is something you have to use to establish a connection into the CloudHSM service. And then you are going to manage the keys overall. So the IAM permissions are going to be used to do a create, read, update, a delete of an HSM cluster at a high level, but then you're going to use your CloudHSM software to manage the keys and manage the users and their permissions to access the keys, which is different from KMS because in KMS, well, everything is managed using IAM.

Now, the CloudHSM clusters can have high availability and they're spread across multiple AZ. So they're HA, and this is super important to understand. So you can have two AZs. One is going to be replicated from another and your HSM client can connect to either. So how do we transparently leverage CloudHSM within the AWS services encryption? Well, there is an integration between CloudHSM and KMS. How does that work? Well, in KMS, we're going to define a KMS custom key store, and that will be CloudHSM.

And that means we can get CloudHSM encryption for EBS, S3, RDS and so on. So how does that work? Well, we create the CloudHSM cluster, and we define a KMS custom key store that is going to be connected to our CloudHSM cluster. From there, if we create an RDS database instance that has an encrypted EBS volume with KMS encryption, well, internally this KMS encryption is going to be leveraging encryption keys within your CloudHSM cluster. The benefit of doing this is number one, we are actually using our CloudHSM cluster.

And number two, any API calls made through KMS that reaches our cloud HSM cluster is going to be logged in CloudTrail. So if we compare CloudHSM and KMS, the tendency of KMS is multi-tenant, whereas for CloudHSM, it's single tenants. They both have the same standard. The master keys are three kinds on KMS, they're AWS owned, AWS managed, and customer managed CMK. Whereas for CloudHSM, it's only customer-managed CMK because AWS cannot access your HSM device.

In terms of key type, it is very similar, symmetric, asymmetric and digital signing for KMS and symmetric, asymmetric and digital sending and hashing for CloudHSM. In terms of key accessibility, well, KMS is accessible in multiple regions, but because CloudHSM is deployed in a VPC, you can share it across VPCs using VPC for sharing. And so that means that it's going to be accessible across multiple regions if you wanted to. For cryptographic acceleration, well, you can set up none on KMS, but with CloudHSM, you have SSL and TLS acceleration you can use at your load balancer level, or you can use Oracle and TDE acceleration as well for your database.

That is Oracle based. For access and authentication, you have IAM for KMS, whereas CloudHSM has its own security mechanism to manage users and their permissions and their keys. And then finally, for high availability, while KMS is a managed service and is always available and CloudHSM will have multiple HSM devices over different availability zones. Other capability is CloudTrail and CloudWatch for KMS, whereas we have MFS support as well for CloudHSM.

Finally, KMS is part of the free tier in AWS, whereas CloudHSM is not. So that's it for CloudHSM, I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: SSM Parameter Store Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about the SSM Parameter Store. It's a secure storage for your configuration and your secrets. And optionally, you can choose to encrypt these configurations and therefore make it secrets by using the KMS service. SSM Parameter Store is serverless, it's scalable, it's durable, and the SDK is very easy to use. On top of it, if you update your parameters then you have version tracking of them. The security is provided through IAM and you get notifications with Amazon EventBridge, in certain amount of cases.

You have full integration with CloudFormation. That means that CloudFormation can leverage the parameters from parameter store as input parameters for your stacks. So let's take an example. We have an application and then we have the SSM parameter store. So we can store plain text configuration in this way. Then the IAM permissions of your applications are going to be checked. For example, your EC2 instance role or you can have encrypted configuration.

In that case the SSM parameter store is going to encrypt it with KMS. And so the KMS service is going to be used for encryption and decryption. And of course, you need to make sure that your applications do have access to the underlying KMS key to perform that encryption and that decryption. So you can store parameters in the parameter store with a hierarchy. So for example, you can define my department as a path and underneath the My-app and then the Dev and then we have the Dev DB-URL and then the DB-password within that folder.

So that means that your parameters goes all the way down into the hierarchy. We can go one level up and store a parameter for the Prod DB-URL, as well as a Prod DB password and go up to another app or another department. That really allows you to organize your parameters the way you want in a structured fashion. And then this is going to simplify your IAM policies to allow applications to have access to an entire department, or to an entire app, or just to an app department environment specific path.

You also have the opportunity to access Secrets of Secrets Manager through the Parameter Store by using this reference right here. So it's a little trick that not many people know. And there are something called Public Parameters that are issued by AWS that you can use. For example, if you want to find the latest AMI for the Amazon Index 2 in your specific region. This is something that's available within the Parameter Store as an API call. So if you take an application, for example our Dev Lambda function is going to have an IAM roll that allows it to access the DB-URL and DB-password within the Dev of my app.

And then if you have a Prod Lambda Function, thanks to again, a different IAM policy and maybe some environment variables, you can access the Prod DB-URL and Prod DB-password of another path. (mouse clicks) Now, within Systems Manager, you have two kinds of parameter tiers. You have the standard and the advanced tier. So the big difference is going to be around the size of 4KB which is 8KB, and also the availability of a parameter policy. For the standard one, we have none but for advanced, we have some.

The advanced type of parameters is going to be a $0.05 per month. Whereas the first one is going to be free. So what are these parameter policies? And this is only for advanced parameters. (mouse clicks) Well, this allows you to assign a time to live to a parameter, that means an expiration date. So that you forced users to update or delete sensitive data such as passwords. And you can assign multiple policies at a time. So here is an example policy.

So this is an expiration policy to delete a parameter and you say, "Hey, on this time stamp you must delete these parameter." And then through the EventBridge integration, EventBridge is going to get notifications of it. So in this example, 15 days before the parameter expires we'll receive notification in EventBridge which gives us enough time to actually update it and make sure the parameter is not getting deleted because of the TTL. Or maybe sometimes you wanna make sure the parameters change once in a while.

So you can have a no change notification in EventBridge so that if a parameter has not been updated for 20 days, then you will be notified as well. So you can get very, you know, creative with the parameter store. But now you get the idea behind it. So I hope you like this lecture and I will see you in the next lecture.
