lectures.title: SSM Parameter Store Hands On (CLI)
lectures.text:
Okay, so let's go ahead and practice using the Parameter Store. So the best way to do it is to type Parameter Store in the search bar, and you can click here. It's a Systems Manager feature. So if you click on Parameter Store, on the left hand side, you will see that under Systems Manager, you have, under Application Tools, the Parameter Store, and what we can do here is create a new parameter. We specify types and values, and then we can reference the parameters in the comments or the code.

So let's go ahead and practice using this service. So I first create a parameter and I need to enter a name for it. So the name is whatever you want. You don't have to follow my direction, but I like to name it like this so /my-app/dev/db-url, and this is going to allow me, with these four slashes to organize them into a hierarchy. So this is my app, this is the Dev Environment, and this is the name of my parameter within the Dev Environment. So here, I say DB Url for the Dev Environment.

That's perfect, and then Tier, we have two options. We have Standard and Advanced. So we are going to use a Standard tier. We can store up to 10,000 standard parameters. They are four kilobytes in value maximum, and we can't share that with other accounts, but the Advanced parameters, you can have 100,000 of them, they can be eight kilobytes and you can share them with your other accounts. So next we're going to choose the type, and the type could be String, StringList, or SecureString.

So here we're going to use String, but later we'll be using SecureString, and if you need to list of string, you can have a StringList, but String here has Data Type. It's either text or AWS EC2 image because you can also reference image ARNs here, and here you just have to specify the text in a specific format. But we'll use Text, and for the string, I will have for example, dev.database.stephantheteacher.com. This is just an example. You don't have to put anything that's a URL.

You can put whatever you want in it, but that's going to be the value of my parameter, this one. So let's create this parameter, and as you can see now it's been created. I can click on it and have a look at it. So this is Version One of this parameter. We can view the version history here. So if I were to change it, then I can of course update it, but I will have access to my version history, which is nice, and then we're going to do the same but add more parameters, so we're going to go under Parameter Store and I'm going to copy this, and here I'm going to have it as db-password, so we're going to create it.

So DB Password for Dev, and as you guessed it, we're going to have a SecureString this time, and because it's a password, we're going to encrypt it with a KMS key, so it could belong in my account or another account. We'll use my account. You could use the default KMS Key ID managed by AWS for the SSM service, which is this one, alias/aws/ssm, or you can select one that you have created before. For example, you may have created, for example, KMS, a key called Tutorial or whatever you want to create it.

You don't have to, and so if you had created it, then you can use it here and leverage it. It's really as you want, but let's choose Tutorial for this example, it doesn't really matter, and we need to put a password, so I'll have it as devpassword, and now this is going to be automatically encrypted by KMS. lectures.title: Secrets Manager - Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about a very simple service called the AWS Secrets Manager. So it's a newer service and it's meant for storing secrets and it's going to be different from the SSM parameter store, because on Secrets Manager, you have the capability to force the rotation of secrets every X number of days, and therefore you have a better secret management schedule. On top of it, from within Secrets Manager, you can force and automate the generation of secrets on the rotation.

And for this, you have to define a Lambda function that will generate that new secrets. Moreover, Secrets Manager is really well integrated with different services on AWS. And I just showed you Amazon RDS for example, for MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL or Aurora. But there are other services as well with AWS, other databases, that are integrated with Secrets Manager out of the box. That means that the username and the password to get into your database is stored directly in Secrets Manager and it can be rotated and so on.

Now, Secrets can be encrypted using the KMS service. And so anytime in the exam you see Secrets, or integration for RDS, or for Aurora of Secrets, really think Secrets Manager. There's one more feature we need to know about which is the concept of multi-region Secrets. So the idea is that you can replicate your Secrets across multiple AWS regions and Secrets Manager Service will keep readers in sync with the primary Secrets. So here have two regions.

We create a Secret in the primary one and it gets replicated as a same Secret into a secondary region. Now, why would we do this? Well, multiple things. Number one, in case there is a problem with US East 1, you're able, for example, to promote a replica Secret as a standalone secret. And then thanks to the fact that that Secret is replicated across regions, then you can build multiple regions apps. You can also have disaster recovery strategies, or if you have an RDS database that is also being replicated from one region to the next, then you can use the same Secret to access, the same, the RDS database, the corresponding one, in the corresponding region.

So that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: SSM Parameter Store vs Secrets Manager
lectures.text:
So let's talk about the differences between the SSM Parameter store and Secrets Manager. So Secrets Manager is more expensive, and you're going to have the automation of the rotation of the secrets using Lambda functions. Some of these Lambda functions are going to be provided out of the box. For example, for RDS, for Redshift, or Document DB, that have strong integrations with Secrets Manager. So it saves you a little bit of time. KMS encryption is going to be mandatory for your secrets and you can integrate them with CloudFormation.

The Parameter Store has a more, has a wider type of use case and is less expensive. It has a simple API. There is no secret rotation, although I will show you in the next slide how you can enable rotation on your own using a Lambda function triggered by EventBridge. KMS encryption is going to be optional because you can store secrets or just parameters in the Parameter Store and it also has integration CloudFormation. And it is possible for you to pull a Secrets Manager from a Secret from Secrets Manager using the SSM Parameter Store API.

This is about events. But, so if we have a look at rotation of secrets between the Parameter Store and Secrets Manager. Well, first for Secrets Manager, say we want to rotate the password of an Amazon RDS database. Therefore, we are going to set up Secrets Manager to automatically invoke every 30 days a Lambda function. Now, this Lambda function, for example, for RDS, is provided by AWS and is deployed in your accounts by AWS. You just need to use it using Secrets Manager.

What it will do is that it will change the password of your Amazon RDS database. So this is a native functionality. And in case it is just a random secret that is not deeply integrated with Secrets Manager, then you need to write your own Lambda function for it. But again, the documentation is provided by AWS. Now, for the SSM Parameter Store, there is no native feature to the rotation. But let's say you were storing an RDS database password into the SSM Parameter Store, then what I would do would be to create an Amazon EventBridge rule that would be invoked every 30 days and that will invoke a Lambda function that you would have to write on your own to change the password of your Amazon RDS database and also to change the value in it that is stored in your SSM Parameter Store.

So hopefully that makes sense into what are the differences between the Secrets Manager and the SSM Parameter Store. I hope you like this lecture and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CloudFormation - Secrets Manager & SSM Integration
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about dynamic references in CloudFormation. So we can store values in Systems Manager Parameter Store or we can store secrets in Secrets Manager. And we can actually reference these values into your CloudFormation templates. The idea is that CloudFormation is going to retrieve the value of the specified references during any create, update or delete operations. lectures.text:
So, one short lecture on the CloudWatch Logs encryption. So, you can encrypt your CloudWatch Logs with KMS keys. And the encryption happens at the log group level. So, not with log streams but the log group level. And that you can either associate a CMK with an existing log group, or you can create a new log group with a CMK. But you cannot associate a CMK with a log group using the CloudWatch console; you have to use the CloudWatch Logs API for the CLI and the SDK, so we'll be using the CLI in this lecture.

And we have two comments to note. The first one is called associate KMS key. To associate a KMS key with an existing log group or create-log-group to create a log group that doesn't exist yet and directly associate it with a KMS key. So, let's go into the hands on to see how that works. So, here I am in CloudWatch Logs. And I'm going to go to my log groups and I have 23 of them right now. And, so, if we take any of those, for example, the aws/lambda/hello-world log group, we can see that there is no KMS key ID associated with that log group yet.

And we can not do any of that through the UI, so the UI does not allow us to associate a KMS key ID with this log group. So, what we want to do is to take this key that we've encrypted from before, the tutorial key, and associate it with this log group. For this we have to use the CLI. So let's go ahead and play it out. So, I'm going to go into my CloudWatch Logs code directory and open this command. And, so, this first command is to associate a KMS key with an existing log group.

I press enter, and I'm getting an access denied exception saying that this associate KNM key operation did not work. Either the key does not exist, but I know it exists for sure, or it's not allowed to be used with this log group, and this is the second options that's right.

So, indeed, the key has not been authorized to be used with this log group. So, we need to apply a certain key policy. So, if we go here, there is a key policy that Jason filed. And we need to apply it to my specific key. So, I'm gonna get the second part here, that's what's interesting. So, I'm gonna get the second part and the comma, and I'm gonna go into my KMS key consul, and in here I have a key policy. I'm going to switch to policy view and I'm going to edit this key policy.

So, this key policy right now is the default key policy which allows any user or role within my account to use my KMS key, but doesn't allow any service. So, we need to allow the service of CloudWatch Logs to access this key. So, I'm going to paste this here, and so there's a comma that has been added in this statement. And, so, here we allow logs dot, and we need to paste in the region, so EU-west-2. So, logs.EU-west-2.amamazonaws.com is allowed to do encrypt, decrypt, re-encrypt, generate data key, and describe on this key.

So, I'll save these changes. And, now I have applied a key policy which should allow more things to access including CloudWatch Log. So, we should try again our command, and, hopefully, this time it will work. So, I will run this command again, and this time it has worked. So, we get the end and it is applied. So, how do I know this? Well, we could refresh this UI and now we can see that out KNS key ID, right here, is associated with out CloudWatch Logs, and so that mean that this log group is going to be fully encrypted with this KMS key ID.

And I could try the second command, which is to create a new log group with this example I called, example encrypted, directly passing in the KMS key ID. So, I paste this in and press enter, and it says end. So, if I go back to my log groups and then refresh, I can find at the very bottom my example encrypted log group. And this one is also associated with out KMS key ID. So, this is the two ways to create an associate KMS key ID with the log groups in CloudWatch Log.

So, it cannot be done through the consul. And I really like the fact that we had to modify a key policy to allow CloudWatch Logs to access out KMS key, which I think is a tremendous example in security. So, that's it for this lecture. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: CodeBuild Security
lectures.text:
Let's do a quick lecture on CodeBuild Security. So first of all, we know that CodeBuild is out of your VPC, but you can launch your CodeBuild inside of your VPC to access your VPC resources. And we haven't talked about secrets in CodeBuild, so obviously do not store them as plaintext in CodeBuild environment variables. That would make no sense. Instead, you have two options. You can have environment variables that reference parameter store's parameters, or environment variables that can reference secrets manager secrets.

And we'll see how to configure this in a second. So, we are in CodeBuild and I'm going to create a new build project. Now, I don't need to fill in any details, I just want to show you where the settings are. So, if I scroll down and go to additional configuration, I have some good configuration regarding security. Number one is regarding the VPC, so we can launch CodeBuild within your VPC, so like the subnets and the security groups. And then if you scroll down, environment variables is super important.

So, say we needed to access, for example, an RDS database within our VPC and we needed the RDS database password. We could say DB_PASSWORD and say "supersecret," but this would be really bad. This is a plaintext secret in your environment, so this could be seen and leaked, so not good. But you can also have a parameter or a secrets manager secret. So, in case of parameter, you can get into the parameter store. So, let me get into the SSM parameter store to show you.

So, in my parameter store, I can create a parameter. I'll call it /CodeBuild/DBPassword. And then I will set it a standard parameter. It's going to be a secure string, and I can say that I want to associate it with this KMS Key ID. So, the AWS CMK, and the value is going to be "SuperSecret" and here we go. Then I'm going to create this parameter, and so now I can reference this parameter name into my value. So here I said DB_PASSWORD is using this value, coming from the parameter store, and automatically at runtime, my CodeBuild will fetch the value of this parameter, so the "SuperSecret" value, which is right here, the "SuperSecret value," and inject it into my container.

But I can also add another one. It could be DB_PASSWORD_ALT, alternative. And you can do the exact same process with the secrets manager by referencing the name of the secret you're looking for in the secrets manager. And of course, if you do these things, make sure that the IM roll associated with your CodeBuild project does have access to the systems manager parameter store and secrets manager. And that's it. Super simple, but some good things to see before the exam.

I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: AWS Nitro Enclaves
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about Nitro Enclaves. So the idea is that sometimes in the cloud you wanna process highly sensitive data, and you wanna process it in an isolated compute environment. So the sensitive data may be, for example, PII data, so personally identifiable information, or healthcare data, financial data, credit card data, whatever you want. And historically, if you wanted to create this very isolated compute environment, you would create a new VPC, you would restrict access to it, you would restrict the networking, and so on, and that would be cumbersome.

So instead, what you can use is Nitro Enclaves. Nitro Enclaves are virtual machines that are super isolated. They're hardened and they're highly constrained. So it's not a container, it doesn't have persistent storage, it doesn't have interactive access, you cannot SSH into it. There's no external networking. So it's really, really contained. And the idea is that this is where you want to do your data processing. So by creating a Nitro Enclave you're going to reduce the attack surface for very sensitive data processing apps.

On top of it, you can make sure that, thanks to Cryptographic Attestation, only authorized code can be running in your Enclave, and you would sign the code and then only the sign code can be running in your Enclave. And on top of it, you can guarantee, thanks to KMS encryption, that only the Enclaves can access your sensitive data. So the use cases for Nitro Enclaves is whenever you want to do private key processing, processing credit cards, or secure multi-party computation, and so on.

So this gives you a highest level amount of security on EC2. So how does that work? Well, you're going to launch a compatible Nitro-based EC2 instance, and you're going to set the 'EnclaveOptions' to 'true' which will allow you to launch from within the EC2 instance, a Nitro Enclave. Then you use a Nitro CLI to convert your app into an Enclave image file, EIF. And then you use this as an input with the Nitro CLI to create an Enclave on your EC2 instance and it will share the VP, the memory, the CPU, and the kernel with the host but it will be very, very isolated within.

So if you consider EC2 Hosts on AWS that is running on the Nitro Hypervisor. This is why it's called Nitro Enclave, is because it leverages the Nitro Hypervisor. Then EC2 instance has separation from your Enclave. They can just communicate over a secure local channel, but that's it. And then there will be of course separation from any other instance running on the same host, but you have the guarantee that the Enclave is going to be as secure as I told you before, with a lot of restrictions on it.

That's it. You just need to know this concept at a high level. But I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service - Overview
lectures.text:
So now, let's talk about the Amazon OpenSearch Service. An Amazon OpenSearch is a successor to something you may have heard before called, Amazon ElasticSearch. So the name change was due to some licensing issues. So in DynamoDB, just to do a comparison, you can only query the data by primary key or if you have indexes on your database. But with OpenSearch, you can actually, as the name indicates, search any fields, even for partial matches. So it's very common to use OpenSearch to provide search to your application.

And so you would use OpenSearch as a compliment to another database. So OpenSearch can be used for search, but also as the name doesn't indicate, you can also do analytic queries on top of OpenSearch. So you have two modes to provision an OpenSearch Cluster. Either you use the managed cluster option and then actual physical instances will be provisioned for you and you will see them. Or you can go the serverless route and have a serverless cluster, where everything from scaling to operations is handled by AWS.

lectures.title: Amazon Athena - Overview
lectures.text:
So now, let's talk about Amazon Athena. So Athena is a serverless query service to help you analyze the data stored in Amazon S3 buckets. And to analyze this data, you're going to use the standard SQL language to query the files. Behind the scenes, Athena is built on the Presto engine, which uses the SQL language. So the idea is that users are going to load data into your S3 bucket, or you are going to load data into your S3 bucket, and then you would use the Athena service to query and analyze this data in Amazon S3 without moving it.

So Athena is serverless, and it analyzes directly your data living in your S3 bucket. So it supports different formats, such as CSV, JSON, ORC, Avro, and Parquet, and possibly others. And the pricing is very simple. You're just going to pay a fixed amount per terabytes of data scanned. You don't need to provision any database again, because the whole service is serverless. So Athena is commonly used with another tool, called Amazon QuickSight to create reports and dashboards.

So we'll see Quicksight later in depth, but Amazon Quicksight connects to Athena, which connects to your S3 buckets. Now, the use cases for Amazon Athena are to do ad hoc queries, business intelligence, analytics, reporting, and to analyze and query any kind of logs that originates from your AWS services. So it could be your VPC flow logs, your load balancer logs, your CloudTrail trails, and so on. So as an exam tip, anytime you need to analyze data in Amazon S3 using a serverless SQL engine, you can think about Athena.

Now, I've talked about performance improvements, and you can actually improve Athena performance, and in this exam, we'll test you on this as well. So first of all, because you pay for the amount of data scanned per terabyte, you need to use a type of data where you're going to scan less data. And for this, you can use a columnar data type for cost-savings, because you only scan the columns you need. So therefore, the recommended formats for Amazon Athena, are going to be Apache Parquet and ORC, and it's going to give you a huge performance improvement.

And to get your files into the Apache Parquet or ORC format, you must use a service that we'll see as well in this section, for example, Glue. Glue can be very helpful to convert your data as an ETL job, between, for example, CSV and Parquet. Now, also because we want to scan less data, we need to compress data for smaller retrievals. So there are different compression mechanisms you can use that have listed it right here. Next, if you know you're going to query all the time on some specific columns, you can partition your datasets, and partition datasets means that in your S3 bucket, you're going to have the full path with slashes, and each slash will be a different column name with a specific value.

And so you're organizing, you're partitioning your data in Amazon S3, so that when you query it, you can know exactly in which folder at which path Amazon S3, you need to scan for data. So here's an example of data partitions. So we have flight data in Parquet formats, and then we do /year=1991. So we partition by year, and we'll have one folder for each year. Then within each year we'll have month, so month equals one, and within each month we'll have days, this equals one.

And so when I do a query on Athena, and I filter for a specific year, a specific month, and a specific day, then we'll know exactly to which folder in Amazon S3 to get the data from, and therefore we'll only recover a subset of the data. Therefore, we'll have really, really good partitioning. Finally, the last performance improvement you need to do, is to use bigger files, it's to minimize your overheads. So if you have many, many, many small files in Amazon S3, Athena is not going to be as performance, as if you had larger files, for example, 128 megabytes, and over, because larger files are easier to scan, and easier to retrieve.

Another feature of Amazon Athena is the Federated Query. So you know that Athena can query data in S3, but actually you can query data anywhere, for example, in relational or non-relational databases, you can query objects and custom data sources, would it be on AWS or on-premises. How? Well, you use what's called a Data Source Connector. It's a Lambda function, and that Lambda function is going to run the Federated Queries in other services. So that could be, for example, CloudWatch Logs, DynamoDB, RDS, and so on.

So it's very powerful. For example, we have Athena here, and we have a Lambda function, and you'll have one Lambda function per Data Source Connector. And then through Amazon Athena, you can run the query across ElastiCache, Document DB, DynamoDB, Redshift, Aurora, SQL Server, MySQL, HBase on the EMR service, or any on-premises database. They're clear from Athena, as well as, of course, Amazon S3, and you can do your drawings, and you can do your competitions, and so on.

That's why it's called a Federated Query. And then the results of this query can be stored into your Amazon S3 buckets for later analysis. So that's it for Amazon Athena. As you can see, it's a very powerful service. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Amazon MSK - Overview
lectures.text:
Another analytics service you will see is Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka, also called Amazon MSK. And what is Kafka? Well, Kafka is an alternative to Amazon Kinesis. Kafka and Kinesis both allow you to stream data. So, MSK is the ability to get a fully-managed Kafka cluster on AWS. And it allows you to create, update and delete clusters on the fly. And MSK is going to create and manage Kafka broker nodes and Zookeeper broker nodes in your cluster for you and you deploy the cluster in your VPC, across multiple AZ, up to three for high availability.

You also have automatic recovery from common Kafka failures and the data is stored on EBS volumes for as long as you want. So, from personal experience, I know it's very difficult to set up Apache Kafka and the fact you can just do one click and then deploy Kafka on AWS is great and this is the Amazon MSK service. So on top of it, you have the option to use MSK Serverless. And this is that you run Apache Kafka on MSK, but this time you don't provision servers, you don't manage capacity, automatically MSK will provision resources and scale, compute and storage for you.

So what is Apache Kafka then? Apache Kafka is a way for you to stream data and a Kafka cluster is made of multiple brokers and then you will have producers that will produce data and so they will have to ingest data from places, such as Kinesis, IoT RDS, et cetera, et cetera, and they will send the data directly into a Kafka topic that is going to be fully replicated into other brokers. Now, this Kafka topic is having real-time streaming of data and consumers will pull from the topic to consume the data itself and then your consumer can do whatever he wants, process it or send it to various destinations, such as EMR, S3, SageMaker, Kinesis and RDS.

So the idea is that Kafka is quite similar to Kinesis, but there are differences to look out for. So what are the differences between Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon MSK? Well, in Kinesis Data Streams, you have one megabyte message limit, which is the default in Amazon MSK, but you can configure it for a higher message retention. For example, 10 megabytes. You can have Data Streams with Shards in Kinesis Data Streams or in MSK, it's called Kafka Topics with Partitions, but the concept are sort of similar.

To scale Kinesis Data Stream, you need to do Shard Splitting and to scale it down Merging. But in Amazon MSK to scale a topic, you can only add partitions. You cannot remove partitions. You have in-flight encryption for Kinesis data streams and then you have either plain text or TLS in-flight encryption for MSK. You get at-risk encryption for both of these clusters and, in the exam level, this is enough. Just so you know, a few differences. And also for Amazon MSK, you can keep data for as long as you want, you can go over one year, as long as you pay for the underlying EBS storage, you're good to go.

Well it's to provide in-fight encryptions for your websites by providing an HTTPS endpoints. So let's take an example. lectures.title: ACM Private CA - Overview
lectures.text:
So we've seen that AWS Certificate Manager can issue public certificates but you can also actually issue private certificates. For this, you must create an AWS Private Certificate Authority. So it's a managed service, and you can create a root Certificate Authority or any subordinaries Certificate Authorities, which are Certificate Authorities that depend on root. So then from there, you can issue and deploy end-entity X.509 certificates, which means that there are certificates that can be used by your applications.

These certificates cannot be used to create new certificates. So these certificates will be trusted only by all your applications within your organization, as long as they trust the Private Certificate Authority. But you cannot deploy these certificates on the public internet. This is just not going to work because it is a Private Certificate Authority. On top of it, if you are using an AWS service that has integration with ACM, for example, your application load balancer, it is completely possible for you to load a certificate on it, that is going to be a private certificate.

So as you can see in this example, I've shown you CloudFront, API Gateway, load balancers, Kubernetes service, and so on. And these certificates can be issued for users for whatever reason, for computers, for your APIs or your HTTP endpoints, and your IoT devices. So the use cases of using a Private Certificate Authority is to have encrypted TLS communication internally, or to cryptographically sign code to authenticate users, computers, API endpoints, and IOT devices by providing them certificates, or to create a public key infrastructure within an enterprise.

So that's it. I hope you liked it. And I will see you in the next lecture.

Now let's talk about Macie. Macie is a fully managed data security and data privacy service that will use machine learning and pattern matching to discover and protect your sensitive data in AWS. More specifically, it will alert you around sensitive data such as personally identifiable information, which is named PII. So very simply, your PII data will be in your S3 buckets and it will be analyzed by Macie which will discover what data can be classified as PII.

And then will notify you through EventBridge of the discoveries. Then you can have integrations into an SNS topic, Lambda functions and so on. So Macie in this instance will be used to find the sensitive data in your S3 buckets and that's the only thing it will do. It's just one click to enable it. You just specify the S3 buckets you want to have and that will be it. So that's it for this lecture, very, very short, but that's enough on Macie. I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: AWS AppConfig - Overview
lectures.text:
So now let's talk about AWS AppConfig. So the idea is that when you configure your applications, it is very common for you to actually ship the configuration alongside your app, and sometimes you can modularize the configuration by using environmental variables. But what if instead you want it to be having the configuration outside of your app? For this, you could use AppConfig, which allows you to configure, validate and deploy dynamic configurations into your applications.

So you can change this configuration and your application will change independently of you deploying any new code to your application. So you don't need to restart your application, everything works dynamically. So the beautiful thing about it is that, for example, you could use feature flags. What is a feature flag? Well say your application comes with a new feature but for now you want to disable it, so you just deploy your application, and in AppConfig you say the feature is off or false.

And then when your application's been deployed and you're ready to test it out, you can just change the feature flag in your AppConfig. Your application will pick it up and automatically this new feature will be enabled. On top of it, you can pretty much dynamically change any kind of configuration, so you can fine tune your application performance and so on. You can, even for example, if you had IP block list or allow list, you can modify them in real time in AppConfig again, without changing your application code.

So it's very useful for apps that you run on EC2 instances, Lambda, ECS, EKS, and so on. On top of it, if you have a configuration change for example, let's go back to our feature flag, you don't want to release the feature to all of your instances at once. You may want to gradually deploy this change to see if you have any issues, and if so, get a rollback. So that's possible with AppConfig as well. So AppConfig has a few config sources. It could be the parameter store, it could be the SSM documents, it could be your SRO buckets or somewhere else.

And then your EC2 instances are, and, of course, the application running on them are going to regularly pull for configuration changes and then pull them. And for example, when we switch change the configuration, automatically we're going to be monitoring with CloudWatch if there is anything going wrong. If so, let's trigger an alarm, and this alarm will trigger a rollback of your configuration. On top of it to make sure that you're not actually distributing a configuration that is wrong.

You can validate it either using a JSON Schema, which is going to check whether or not the config adheres to some specific types and so on, or a Lambda function. This is when you want to have code and this code is going to check the parameters in a more complex way. And that's it, that's AppConfig. I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

lectures.title: Exam Tips - AWS Certified Developer Associate
lectures.text:
So, here are my tips and my two cents to pass the exam, so it's just general advice. Probably some of this is obvious, some of it you just need to hear once. To me, the number one tip is practice makes perfect. So, if you're new to AWS, it will take a lot of practice to understand how to work with AWS on a daily basis. If you're new to AWS, this course probably gives you massive head start into using AWS. If you feel confident, then do the exam, if not, don't rush, you have time.

Just work on AWS, be confident. Use IAM rolls, deploy applications, and then when you're ready, you can take the exam. The exam recommends you will each have one or more years of hands-on experience. So, there are things you can't fake, so up to you to see if you're ready or not to pass the exam. So, what I say is practice makes perfect! And, a feeling you might have right now is overwhelmed by the amount of knowledge I just threw at you, that you just learned.

So, it takes time to have knowledge, this is not the kind of course you'd do in three days. This is the kind of course that goes over weeks. And, so if you have a lot of acquired knowledge, but you don't think it's perfect yet in your mind, then start practicing and do the course one more time. It's a few hours, obviously, but it will really help you not to waste the exam cost afterwards. So, really just practice. That's my advice. So, if you want to practice, you may be like, how do I do this?

Well, if you're in a company, then good, just work with your company. If not, then take one of your existing applications in whatever language you want. Try to deploy it manually in EC2. That's be a good first step. Then, try to deploy it on Elastic Beanstalk and have it scale with a little downserver and a scaling group. Maybe create a CICD pipeline for it. So you go all the way from your code to your artifacts to the deployments. Maybe you can try breaking down your application to several components and use SQS and SNS to decouple your whole application.

If possible, if you use java, go python, node, these kind of languages, then you can run it with AWS Lambda and its friends. So, it's friends of DynamoDB, API gateway. So that, maybe involve a bit of refactoring, but it could be fun. And, if you want to practice with the CLI and the SDK, I would strongly recommend to have ideas like this. So, for example, create a script or create CLI or SDK script that will shut down your EC2 instances at night and start them in the morning.

That's actually a fun project to do on your own. Or, you can have one that automates snapshots of your EBS volumes at night, so you know they're always backed up once a day. And, maybe an idea three is to list under-utilized EC2 instances in one region. And maybe under-utilize them in CPU Utilization under 10 percent, so that you don't waste money on under-utilized EC2 instances for example. Again, just a bunch of ideas, you may have your own ideas, based on your used cases, or what you do in your daily basis.

But, what I want to do is just give you leads onto practicing. Now, for the exam, you're going to have questions and you're going to have multiple answers, sometimes one answer, sometimes more than one answer. Most of these questions are going to be scenario based. And, for all the questions, I would suggest to start by ruling out answers that you know for sure are wrong. So, it's a really good way to start, to getting started, because if you know something is wrong, then you eliminate it, and that's one less question you have to think, answer you have to think about.

So, for the remaining answers, you need to really think about which one makes the most sense. And, honestly, I'll be very honest with you, there are very few trick questions, so don't overthink your whole process. If one answer makes a lot of sense, then go for it. If one answer seems feasible, but is very complicated, and requires a lot of engineering, it's probably wrong. Sometimes there are two answers that are correct, but one really is easier than the other, or makes more sense, so really use your sound judgment.

Try to think about how much effort it would be for you to implement whatever the question asks you to do, and make a decision based on that. But usually, proceeding by elimination and then using your judgment and your knowledge really makes you go through most of the questions. Remember, there are very, very few trick questions. And, the questions will have key words that will indicate usually something that will be determining in the answer. If for example, serverless probably means AWS, Lambda, and DynamoDB, and API Gateway.

That type of stuff. Now, the AWS Whitepapers, they recommend you to read them. To be honest, it is 10 whitepapers of 40 pages, you may not want to read them all, but you should skim them. So, there's lot of white papers, you know, it's Security Best Practices, so using IAM rolls, that kind of stuff, encryption, we've seen this. Then the Well-Architected Framework. So, around how you architecture applications, segregation of duties using RDS, ElastiCache, et cetera.

Architecting for the Cloud, which is kind of the same thing. The CICD paper is going to be around CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, CodePipeline, CodeCommit. We've seen this in large. Microservices on the AWS is going to be around AWS Lambda, and also ECS, and also all these things to decouple your microservices and have them innovate with one another. Serverless Architecture with AWS Lambda, I think we've seen a lot of it, and we we've also seen the SAM framework, which will be discussed in there.

Optimizing Enterprise Economics with Serverless Architectures basically explains you that if you go Serverless, then you don't have to pay people to manage and do maintenance of your stuff, and so you save a lot of money. And on top of it, Serverless means that you only pay for what you use, so you should be optimal in pricing. Now, Containerized Microservices on AWS. This is an advanced topic, but this is around ECS. Basically it's saying okay, use docker in ECS to deploy microservice on AWS.

Remember the exam only is asking you about a high level of of ECS not a deep dive. Blue/Green Deployments, I've tried to place that everywhere alongside the course, there's going to be blue/green deployments on Beanstalk, maybe there's a bit of blue/green deployments on Lambda or API Gateway. All this stuff we've seen, blue/green is basically testing the new version, the green version, while the blue version is still running. And then when we're ready, switching over from the blue version to the green version.

Overall, I feel that we've explained the, explored the most important concepts in this course, but if you feel strongly about one of these papers, and you want to read about it, then go for it. I think they're very interesting, each of these papers. The one paper you might want to have a peak into is the Blue/Green Deployments on AWS, just you have a quick look, but don't overthink it. The most of the questions, and probably all the questions are going to be covered by this course already.

Now each service will have an FAQ, so frequently asked questions. So, for example for Lambda its /lambda/faqs. And I think they're very important because FAQ covers a lot of the questions they will ask you at the exam, and they may help you confirm your understanding of a service, or maybe shed some light on a doubt you may have. So, definitely look at the Service FAQs, especially the one you don't really understand. Now, lastly, is really around community, so you need to get into the AWS community, you need to talk to other Amazon engineers.

You know, talking to people really unlocks knowledge, at least for me it does. So, discuss with other people in the course Q&A. Definitely help other people answering their questions. And by answering their questions, this is how you learn, you learn by teaching. And you review questions, asked by other people. Definitely look at what other people's concerns were. Maybe they will help you. Maybe the answers will, again, teach you a few stuff. And, do the practice test in this section, just to see where you are at.

You should read forums online. If you are very curious, read online blogs and also there are local meetups to discuss with other Amazon Engineers. Finally, if you are more of a YouTube person, there are a lot of re-invent videos that are quite nice. The re-invent is an AWS Conference, and they have a lot of good content out there. Basically a presentation of their service, and sometimes a little demo. So, that's it, really for the tips of what you need to do.

I believe you're ready, but it's up to you to see how much more practice you want to have. But, yeah hopefully these tips help and I will see you in the next lecture.
